As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater. Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet. All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
abstract: Policy AI News Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.﻿ While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.﻿ by Lauren Feiner Nov 20, 2026, 6:50 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Part Of All the latest updates on AI data centers see all updates Lauren Feiner is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform. President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them. “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.” Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.” Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative. Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks: Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside. We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind. So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them. title: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
abstract: AI News Science Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics. An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics. by Robert Hart and Emma Roth Nov 20, 2026, 4:34 PM UTC If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Anthropic went public on November 19th, 2026. Photo: Getty Images Part Of All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics see all updates Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field. Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website , Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday . The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics. A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof: I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof 1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August , but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.” Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules , a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.” In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture , a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids. OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude. OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar. Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape. title: The week everything fell apart
abstract: Podcasts AI Policy The week everything fell apart On The Vergecast: Is AI breaking the world? And is Jensen Huang coming back to Nvidia? On The Vergecast: Is AI breaking the world? And is Jensen Huang coming back to Nvidia? by David Pierce Nov 20, 2026, 2:06 PM UTC David Pierce is editor-at-large and Vergecast co-host with over a decade of experience covering consumer tech. Previously, at Protocol, The Wall Street Journal, and Wired. There was a dayslong Outlook outage . A nationwide ground stop for only the second time in 25 years. Banks seemed to suddenly stop working . Even iCloud couldn’t stay up and running . This week, it felt like the technological world simply collapsed. And it felt like this might be the beginning of something even bigger. On this episode of The Vergecast , Nilay and David go through the week’s many calamities, and try to explain both what happened in each case — which was generally much milder than the conspiracy theories would have you believe — and why all these small issues might still add up to something worth worrying about. In a world filled with more AI and fewer humans, we’re going to see new kinds of problems and often struggle to find the fixes. After that, the hosts discuss the latest in the Jensen Huang / Nvidia scandal, which is increasingly less about affairs and more about the allegedly very big business of illegally smuggling chips to China . Huang will not be back as Nvidia CEO anytime soon, no matter what a bunch of X users want , and the fallout of his exit seems likely to only increase. Finally, in the lightning round, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy , Nilay’s experience with his always-listening Apple Watch , Google’s inability to name products , and much more. title: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
abstract: AI News Tech Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen Signal will now restrict screenshots on mobile devices, and says AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy.’ Signal will now restrict screenshots on mobile devices, and says AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy.’ by Jess Weatherbed Nov 20, 2026, 12:30 PM UTC Signal users on iOS will see this option to toggle blocking screenshots and preventing Siri AI from scanning on-screen content. Image: Signal Jess Weatherbed is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews. Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post , while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access. “We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.” Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri , Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot-blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device file system. Signal’s app security settings on Android devices will display this message for the screenshot-blocking feature. Image: Signal Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data. “We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Hebbia sees improvements in financial research with GPT-6 Astra
abstract: November 20, 2026 Hebbia sees improvements in financial research with GPT‑6 Astra Hebbia sees gains in financial research in tests of GPT‑6 Astra. Join the community Company size: Startup Region: North America Industry: Technology Products: API Required source types cited 13.6 Percentage-point lead over the best alternative tested in Hebbia’s tests. Citation relevance 99.5 Percent of cited excerpts relevant to the question in Hebbia’s tests. Presentation requirements met 97.9 Percent of applicable presentation requirements met in Hebbia’s tests. Presentation requirement lead 14.4 Percentage-point lead over the best alternative tested on presentation requirements. Share Before a banker can recommend an acquisition to their client, they need to make sense of financial statements, customer contracts and management presentations. Hebbia’s Matrix helps bring that research together, linking answers to the documents behind them. Hebbia tested OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra to improve two parts of that work: finding the sources a question requires and building a presentation that follows the banker’s brief. “We’ve been strong partners with OpenAI over the course of Hebbia’s lifetime, and the leaps GPT-6 Astra has made in terms of quality outputs and accuracy have truly been surprising. GPT-6 Astra shines compared to any other model we’ve tested before on these two fronts.” —Kavita Anand, Member of Technical Staff, Product, Hebbia From source documents to presentations It could work like this: a banker is helping their client assess a strategic acquisition of an industrial-software company, with roughly 2,000 files to review. What makes its revenue durable? How does it compare with peers? In Hebbia’s hypothetical example, the banker could load the data room into Matrix and examine customer concentration, contract terms and churn in cited cells. Matrix could bring in peer filings and industry news to help develop the deal thesis, then turn that research into a diligence summary and valuation deck in the firm’s template. In that workflow, GPT‑6 Astra selects documents or Matrix cells to support an answer, then turns the analysis into native PowerPoint slides that follow the user’s structure and guidelines. “Traceability is really important to our users because they’re basing millions of dollars of decisions on what the AI actually comes back with,” Kavita says. “Citations help with traceability as well as giving users confidence that the AI found the right answer.” In Hebbia’s tests, GPT‑6 Astra combined broader source coverage with highly relevant citations. It scored 13.6 percentage points above the best alternative tested on citing the required types of sources, while 99.5% of the excerpts it cited were relevant to the question. Hebbia tested a prerelease build in August-September 2026, using the same financial research cases and grading criteria for each model. Domain experts wrote or audited the criteria against source documents. “When you’re looking at a data room with thousands of documents, that’s extremely important. Even a single percentage-point gain can yield a lot of marginal benefit,” Kavita says. A presentation also has to look like work the banker would send to a client. “I don’t want to create a deck and send that to my partner that looks like AI made it,” Kavita says. “I want it to be made in my firm’s branding, and I want it to look like a human-made slide.” GPT‑6 Astra led on both following the brief and presentation quality. In Hebbia’s tests, it met 97.9% of the applicable presentation requirements, putting it 14.4 percentage points ahead of the best alternative tested on that measure. Other models traded off polish and adherence to the brief; GPT‑6 Astra ranked first on both. “In the past, we’ve seen models that really shine on one or the other of these dimensions where they’re really good at craft, but the instruction following and adhering to guidelines is not strong, or vice versa. GPT‑6 Astra is the first model we’ve seen where it’s number one on both of those fronts,” Kavita says. In Hebbia, users can open a citation to see the underlying document and highlighted passage; slide footnotes lead back to the source material, too. A review could be as specific as checking a customer-concentration figure against the source table and correcting the reporting period before the deck goes to the investment committee. Hebbia wants bankers to spend less time reformatting decks and checking sources, and more time assessing a deal. Kavita describes what a better first draft could make possible: “What’s amazing about GPT-6 Astra is its ability to create really precise outputs and artifacts that adhere to user guidelines. You can imagine the hours this will save professionals when you get a deck that is closer to your final output. The overnighters that you have to pull get reduced to a few minutes of reviewing GPT-6 Astra’s output.” —Kavita Anand, Member of Technical Staff, Product, Hebbia A future role for agents Kavita sees a future role for agents that monitor information in the background and surface signals for finance professionals to assess. “Imagine getting an important signal a few hours before your competitors,” she says. “You can get started thinking about it and see and process more opportunities that a human is not manually hunting. It can unlock a lot of value for our users.” Hebbia wants to build on these results to help finance professionals assess deals with research they can trace back to its sources. title: Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates?
abstract: November 20, 2026 Research Release Science Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates? Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next. Read the paper (opens in a new window) 00:00 Share We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines. One of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. For AI to help, it needs to connect changes in molecular structure with experimental evidence and reason about what compounds are worth pursuing. MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model. What MedChemBench grades MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings. The benchmark evaluates four components: Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided. Scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another. Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements. Property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties. Prediction across competing properties One MedChemBench problem draws on research into inhibitors of PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. The model receives molecular structures and results from earlier experiments. It must predict how three related compounds will behave: how strongly they block PRMT5 in cells, how readily they cross a cell barrier, and how quickly liver enzymes break them down in a laboratory assay. Later experiments, withheld from the model, showed a tradeoff. Compound 23 blocked PRMT5 in cells at a lower concentration, while compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay. Predicting these properties together tests whether a model can connect molecular structures with several aspects of compound behavior. This reflects a central challenge in medicinal chemistry: stronger activity against a target does not necessarily come with better permeability or slower breakdown. The benchmark checks whether the model reconstructs the molecular structures correctly and how closely its predictions match experimental measurements. Predictions receive partial credit based on their closeness to the measured values. Measurements already supplied in the prompt must also be reproduced correctly. 00:00 Small chemical changes can produce different property profiles. The task asks models to connect the structures with evidence about their behavior. Testing spatial reasoning in medicinal chemistry Before a model can reason about a compound’s properties, it needs to identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connections, ring structures, and stereochemistry. MedChemBench tests whether models preserve this information when reconstructing molecules from the drawings and chemical groups provided. One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At the highest reasoning setting shared by all eleven models (xhigh), GPT‑6 Astra reconstructed this compound correctly in all ten responses. GPT‑5.6 Sol and GPT‑5.6 Luna failed across all ten responses. In the illustrated answers, GPT‑5.6 Sol produced a 15-atom ring, while GPT‑5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected fragments. These errors change the identity of the molecule being analyzed. This example tests a foundation of medicinal chemistry reasoning: whether the model can accurately represent the compound before interpreting its behavior. Figure 1. The same input, different molecules These selected answers for compound 17 show a correct reconstruction, a smaller ring, and disconnected fragments. While measuring the benchmark for structure components, Astra earned 95.4% of the available credit at xhigh. This result shows strong performance on reconstructing the molecular structures supplied in the tasks. We evaluated eleven GPT models at different reasoning-effort settings. Across the full benchmark, Astra earned 83.3% of the available credit at the shared xhigh setting, compared with 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT‑6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. At max effort, GPT‑6 Astra reached 83.8%. Higher reasoning settings improved scores, while large differences between models remained. The figure below plots performance against output tokens. Figure 2. Performance versus token usage Each point represents a model at one reasoning setting, showing 51 combinations across nine models from GPT‑5.6 onward. Scores are averaged across 99 problems; bars show 95% uncertainty intervals. Tokens include reasoning and the final answer. The component results separate four abilities: reconstructing molecules, explaining findings, selecting compounds, and predicting measurements. This shows where models are strongest and where errors remain. Figure 3. Component performance versus token usage Astra’s clearest strengths were in reconstructing molecular structures and explaining the scientific evidence. In selected reasoning examples from our preprint, Astra correctly identified structural changes and weighed their possible effects on protein binding, absorption, and metabolism. Where selection and prediction remain difficult, Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh, but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. These categories use different tasks and scoring rules, but the results show substantial room to improve predictions and compound choices. Where we go from here These results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out, and each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments. While the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery, its results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain. We believe MedChemBench will support continued progress and look forward to sharing updates as our models advance to serve the field. 2026 Author OpenAI Keep reading View all Research acceleration: The jagged frontier Research Nov 18, 2026 Advancing chip design with OpenAI models Research Nov 18, 2026 Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol Product Nov 17, 2026

Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost
abstract: Back to Articles Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost Published November 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 25 +19 Younes B ybelkada Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Nathan Habib SaylorTwift Follow Lysandre lysandre Follow Amine Dirhoussi aminediroHF Follow Adithya S K AdithyaSK Follow shaun smith evalstate Follow Sergio Paniego sergiopaniego Follow Joel Niklaus joelniklaus Follow Lewis Tunstall lewtun Follow Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution. Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination. Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time. Our earlier work ( multi-harness RL , harness adapters ) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations. TL;DR We trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B per agent harness (pi, Hermes Agent, OpenCode), with RL inside the harness itself. Datasets, training and agent rollouts all happen on the Hub in Jobs using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer , OpenEnv and harbor. Each harness adapter beats the base model under its own harness on both benchmarks, for both performance and efficiency. The three LoRAs are also merged into a single super adapter that runs unchanged under pi, Hermes Agent and OpenCode. All artifacts (adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, safeagents plugin) can be browsed through this Hugging Face collection . Table of Contents Training inside agent harnesses Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face Testing the filters with short training runs AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training Training setup Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one Final results Open question: What did the model really learn to do? Closing words and future directions Training inside agent harnesses We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2 , OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6 . The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol: Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop , SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM 's agent and environment classes, slime 's custom rollout functions, or ART 's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer. Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv . We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains. RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything. This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate , and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B. Three sources Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves: SWE-smith ( Python , Go ) injects bugs into real Python and Go repositories, with an LLM rewrite or a mutation such as a flipped operator. The tests that catch each bug become the task's tests. It adds volume. SWE-Gym, packaged as Harbor tasks in TaskTrove , turns real GitHub issues and their merged fixes into tasks. It adds real-world bugs. Tasksmith generates tasks from merged pull requests. An LLM agent writes the instruction and tests, and Tasksmith checks the result: the reference and a valid alternative must pass, while the unfixed code and a known-wrong solution must fail. We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest. Validation with openenv validate A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials: The reference solution earns the maximum reward ( semantic.oracle_max ). Doing nothing scores clearly lower ( semantic.floor_gap ). No canary scores more than doing nothing ( semantic.canary_floor ). A replay of the reference gives the same reward ( runtime.episode_determinism ). Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task: openenv validate path/to/task --sandbox hf-sandbox 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded. Difficulty check with the base model A valid task can still teach nothing.

title: RadixArk Ships DaisyRose-27B, a 27B Agentic Coding Model Trained With Reinforcement Learning Only
abstract: This week RadixArk released DaisyRose-27B , its first open-weight model. DaisyRose-27B is an agentic coding model from RadixArk, post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B with reinforcement learning (RL). The model card page states that it used RL only, with no SFT or distillation. It ships under Apache 2.0 as a drop-in replacement for the base model. The main result: Terminal Bench 4.1 pass@1 rises from 5.6 to 12.0. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . DaisyRose-27B keeps the Qwen3.8-27B architecture unchanged. The model card lists 64 decoder layers in a 3:1 pattern. Three Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers alternate with 1 full-attention layer. Hidden size is 5,120. A 27-layer vision encoder handles images. One multi-token-prediction layer supports speculative decoding. Input is text and images, output is text, and it is a thinking model. RadixArk built about 1,200 curated tasks with Eigent AI , chosen from thousands of candidates. Each task targets a specific failure of the base model. Each sandbox attempt allows up to 1.5 hours, 100+ tool calls and 256k+ output tokens. Agent sessions reach up to 1M tokens, per the blog . Training ran on Miles , RadixArk’s open-source RL framework, in fully asynchronous mode. The run used 144 H200 GPUs for 18 days. Of those, 128 handled agent inference and 16 handled training. Total compute was 63,000 GPU-hours. RadixArk reports 37% MFU on its internal backend. An open-source Megatron-based trainer reached 16%. End-to-end throughput was 16.8k tokens/s versus 8.3k, a 2.0x speedup. RadixArk says this cut GPU time by 57%. Sandboxes ran on AgentENV . RadixArk reports about 944,000 sandboxes from mid-September to mid-November. Peak concurrency hit 1,566. Creation success was 99% over 9 weeks. RadixArk puts the cost about 80% below popular cloud sandbox providers. All scores are self-reported by RadixArk. DaisyRose scores are the higher of its BF16 and FP8 runs. Source: RadixArk blog and model card . The largest jump is Terminal Bench 4.1, which more than doubles. Coding gains are steady: +4.0 on DeepSWE v1.1 and +3.4 on SWE Bench Pro v2. Knowledge gains are small, at +0.4 on HLE and +1.5 on GPQA Diamond. Against larger models, results are mixed. MiMo V2.6 Flash (309B total) leads Terminal Bench 4.1 at 16.1. Inkling 2 Small (594B total) leads DeepSWE at 72.1 and HLE at 44.1. DaisyRose-27B tops RadixArk’s 9-model table only on IFBench. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16 , FP8 , NVFP4 and GGUF . NVFP4 requires a Blackwell GPU. RadixArk recommends SGLang with DSpark speculative decoding. That setup uses the Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark draft model. vLLM also works via vllm serve "RadixArk/DaisyRose-27B" . Suggested thinking-mode sampling is temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 and top_k 20. *From RadixArk’s comparison table , which cites each developer’s reports or leaderboards. SWE Bench Pro v2 figures trace to arXiv 2611.16289 . The last row comes from each model’s own card. Check out the model card , the technical blog and the Miles repo . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. title: NVIDIA AI Releases Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, a Continuous Diffusion Language Model with 14 checkpoints at 3B/8B
abstract: NVIDIA has released Nemotron-Labs-Sigma , a collection of 14 open checkpoints at 3B and 8B scale. Nemotron-Labs-Sigma is a continuous diffusion language model family that denoises text in a 16-D embedding space. Most diffusion LLMs, such as LLaDA and Dream, work on discrete tokens. Sigma works in a smooth latent space instead. NVIDIA team states that this makes few-step distillation and trajectory steering practical for text. The research team calls Sigma the first large-scale family of continuous diffusion language models. The collection has 4 variant types at each size: Each token maps to a point in a learned 16-D embedding space . Training adds Gaussian noise to these embeddings and teaches the model to remove it. The embedding geometry is learned jointly with the denoiser. Generation runs blockwise. Each denoised block is committed to a KV cache before the next starts. Blocks default to 64 tokens. The backbone is a Ministral-style decoder-only Transformer with grouped-query attention, SwiGLU and rotary embeddings. Training starts from an autoregressive warm start of about 1T tokens. About 0.3T tokens of diffusion training follow. At inference, classifier-free guidance and score temperature matter most. The model card page recommends guidance 3 and temperature 0.3 at 32 DDIM steps. Discrete diffusion jumps between token states, so its trajectories are hard to steer. Sigma follows smooth ODE/SDE paths instead. Per the research paper , these degrade gracefully at low step counts and distill efficiently. Embedding-space steering also tunes the quality-diversity trade-off for pass@k sampling. On the research’s 6-task base suite, Sigma-8B with 256 DDPM steps averages 71.16. NLD-8B in diffusion mode scores 70.22, Dream-7B 58.74 and LLaDA-8B 41.78. Qwen3-8B in AR mode scores 68.91. A cheaper 32-step DDIM sampler still gives Sigma-8B a 70.18 average. Coding is the standout. Sigma-8B scores 65.12 on HumanEval versus 62.80 for NLD-8B. MBPP is weaker, at 65.74 versus 67.00. After SFT, Sigma-8B-instruct scores 91.96 on GSM8K, 78.40 on MATH-500 and 82.50 on HumanEval. Hard reasoning stays limited, at 23.33 on AIME24 and 17.00 on AIME25. Its 10-task average of 59.14 sits just below NLD-8B at 59.92. All scores are NVIDIA’s own evaluations. Sigma-distill-8B-nfe8 decodes each 32-token block in 8 denoiser calls plus 1 readout. Its card reports a 6-task mean of 70.34, with 88.44 on GSM8K and 65.18 on HumanEval. That is close to the 256-step teacher. NVIDIA’s launch thread frames the gain as 8 tokens per forward on math and 4 on code. The distill-spec checkpoints add self-speculative decoding. A diffusion head drafts a 32-token block, and the model’s own AR head verifies it. Output exactly matches greedy AR decoding. On 1 GB200 with SGLang, the 8B spec model runs 3.46x faster than AR decoding on average. NLD-8B reaches 3.04x on the same setup. Peak speedups reach 4.20x at 8B and 3.18x at 3B. All 14 checkpoints are on Hugging Face under the NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License. The cards state the models are ready for commercial use. You need a CUDA GPU in bfloat16: Ampere, Lovelace, Hopper or Blackwell. CPU inference is not supported. Loading needs PyTorch 2.4+, Transformers 4.55+ and trust_remote_code . On 1 H100, the base model generates about 120 to 140 tokens/s. The distilled card lists vLLM, SGLang and Docker Model Runner for serving. NVIDIA hosts no API. Benchmark rows use NVIDIA’s evaluations from the Sigma paper (Table 2 base, Table 5 instruct). Specs come from each model’s own card. Check out the Paper , Model Collection and Project Page . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. title: Open Source vs. Proprietary LLMs: A Decision Framework for 2026
abstract: Open Source vs. Proprietary LLMs: A Decision Framework for 2026 A practical guide to choosing between open-weight and commercial models, built around the four questions that actually determine the right answer for your use case. By Vinod Chugani on November 20, 2026 in Language Models "Should we use an open source or proprietary large language model (LLM)?" The answer in 2026 looks very different from what it did eighteen months ago. The capability gap between the two categories has shrunk considerably. Cost dynamics now favor open models at scale but still tilt toward proprietary APIs for low-volume work and rapid iteration. And the practical factors — data privacy, fine-tuning needs, infrastructure capacity, and regulatory compliance — carry more weight than raw benchmark scores in most real-world decisions. This guide doesn't argue for one category over the other. Both are legitimate, and both are widely deployed in production. The goal is to give data scientists and machine learning engineers a structured framework for making the decision based on what actually matters for their situation, not what generates the most online commentary. The framework boils down to four questions: What does your data sensitivity require? What's your usage volume? How much do you need to customize the model? And what can your team's infrastructure handle? Working through those four questions will resolve the open-vs-proprietary decision for the vast majority of use cases. Understanding the Current Model Families Before we get into the decision framework, here's what each category actually contains in 2026. The Open-Weight Landscape "Open source" in the LLM context usually means open-weight. The model weights are publicly available, but the training data, code, and methodology may not be fully disclosed. Licensing terms vary a lot, and some licenses marketed as open source don't meet the Open Source Initiative's formal definition. Here are the leading open-weight model families in 2026: Meta's Llama 4 family remains the most influential open-weight series. Llama 4 Scout stands out with a 10 million token context window, the first open model to hit that scale, making it a real contender for long-context document analysis. The Llama license (Meta Community License) permits commercial use but includes restrictions worth reading carefully before deployment. DeepSeek has established itself as one of the most capable open-weight providers. DeepSeek V3 and its successors benchmark favorably against GPT-4o class models on reasoning and coding tasks. DeepSeek R1 is specifically built for mathematical and logical reasoning, making it the strongest open-weight pick for tasks involving complex multi-step inference. The MIT license is the most permissive of the major open-weight families. Qwen 3.5 (Alibaba) currently sits at the top of several open-weight leaderboards for overall reasoning and coding. The 235B-A22B mixture-of-experts variant goes toe-to-toe with frontier proprietary models on most standard benchmarks. Apache 2.0 licensing makes it commercially accessible. Qwen 3.5 also leads in multilingual performance, especially for Chinese, Arabic, and other non-English languages. Mistral contributes a range of efficient open-weight models, with Mistral Small variants punching above their weight class. Smaller Mistral models (Mistral 7B and Mistral Small) carry Apache 2.0 licenses. Mistral's French origin gives it particular relevance for organizations operating under European data governance frameworks, and Mistral Small 4 fits well into GDPR-aligned EU deployment scenarios. The Proprietary API Landscape Proprietary models are accessed through managed APIs. No weights are available. The provider handles infrastructure, updates, and scaling. The leading proprietary models in 2026 include the GPT-5 series from OpenAI , Claude models from Anthropic , and Gemini models from Google . Each has distinct strengths. Claude's 200K token context window is a clear advantage for long-document analysis. GPT-5's ecosystem depth (SDKs, integrations, structured output formats, Assistants API) makes it the lowest-friction choice for teams already building on OpenAI tooling. Gemini integrates tightly with Google Cloud and Vertex AI, which benefits organizations already in that ecosystem. Proprietary API pricing in 2026 spans a wide range, from \$0.05 per million input tokens for lightweight models up to \$30 per million for frontier-tier models. The mid-tier most commonly used in production (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet, Gemini Flash) runs between \$1.25 and \$3.00 per million input tokens. Output tokens cost two to four times the input rate. One big shift in 2026: LLM API pricing has dropped roughly 80% since early 2023, driven by competition from open-weight models and efficiency improvements. Frontier proprietary models still command a 2–5x price premium over equivalent open-weight models accessed through hosted inference providers. The Performance Reality Before working through the framework, it helps to understand what the capability gap actually looks like so you can gauge how much it matters for your specific use case. The big picture: open-weight models have closed 70–90% of the capability gap against frontier proprietary models as measured by standard benchmarks. On specific task categories like coding, structured data extraction, and mathematical reasoning, the best open-weight models match or sometimes exceed proprietary alternatives. The persistent gaps show up in complex multi-step reasoning (where Claude Opus-class models still lead on benchmarks like GPQA Diamond), instruction-following consistency at scale, and performance in low-resource languages. Here's the practical takeaway: for about 80% of data science use cases (text classification, summarization, structured data extraction, retrieval-augmented generation over internal documents, code generation assistance), well-chosen open-weight models deliver results that are functionally indistinguishable from proprietary APIs. For the remaining 20% — which includes nuanced long-form reasoning, complex agentic chains, or applications where output reliability at the tail end matters a lot — proprietary frontier models still hold a measurable edge. Bottom line: evaluate models on your actual tasks, not on published leaderboard scores for tasks you'll never run in production. Open source vs proprietary LLMs decision framework for 2026 (click to enlarge). The Four-Question Decision Framework Question 1: What Does Your Data Require? This is the question that settles the debate most often, and it has nothing to do with cost or capability. If your use case involves data that cannot legally or contractually leave your environment, open-weight self-hosting isn't just an option. It's a requirement. The categories that trigger this include medical records and clinical notes (HIPAA in the US, similar regulations elsewhere), personal financial information (PII, transaction data, account details), proprietary business data under NDA or confidentiality agreements, government and defense data with classification or sovereignty requirements, and EU personal data under GDPR when the API provider's data processing arrangements don't satisfy your legal team. If you fall into any of these categories, the decision branches straight to open-weight self-hosting or a private cloud deployment. Cost and capability comparisons take a back seat because compliance isn't negotiable. If your data can be sent to a third-party API provider (most general business text, public data, anonymized datasets), move on to Questions 2 through 4. Question 2: What Is Your Usage Volume? The cost math for open-weight vs. proprietary APIs isn't linear. It depends heavily on scale. At low volume (under 1 million tokens per month), proprietary APIs are more cost-effective once you factor in the infrastructure and engineering overhead of running your own models.

title: Decision AI Explained in 5 Minutes
abstract: Decision AI Explained in 5 Minutes Learn how decision models work, how they turn LLMs into faster decision-making systems, and how to run open-source alternatives locally. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on November 20, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Not every AI task needs a large language model (LLM) that generates text. Sometimes, we just need a model to make a quick decision, such as choosing the right tool, classifying a customer complaint, or deciding whether a transaction looks suspicious. This is where Decision AI comes in. With the release of Jev by TypeSafe AI and several open-source alternatives, we now have models specifically designed to make these decisions without generating unnecessary text. In this article, we will learn how Decision AI works, explore open-source models, and run our first decision model locally using llama.cpp . What Is Decision AI? Decision AI is the use of AI to help make decisions. It is a broad field, but a newer generation of decision models focuses on something quite simple: instead of generating text, the model selects from predefined answers and returns probabilities. These models generally support three types of questions: Choice: Select an option, such as billing, sales, or technical support. Score: Rate something on a scale, such as the urgency of a customer complaint. Yes or no: Estimate whether something is true, such as whether an email is spam. For example, imagine a customer sends an email saying, "I was charged twice for my order." We don't need an LLM to write a lengthy explanation. A decision model can simply identify billing as the most appropriate department and return a probability for that answer. This makes decision models useful for applications that process thousands of similar requests. How Does Decision AI Work? The process is straightforward. We provide the model with some information, define a question, and specify the possible answers. The model evaluates the information and returns its decision with probabilities. Here is a simple workflow: Going back to our customer support example, an illustrative result might look like this: Question Answer Probability Which department? Billing 92% Is it urgent? Yes 81% Does it need human review? No 76% These are hypothetical results. In practice, we would test the model's accuracy and probabilities on real customer messages before automating anything. The main advantage is that the answers are structured, so our application can use them directly without extracting information from generated paragraphs. Turning Large Language Models Into Decision Models We can turn an existing LLM into a decision model by using its internal predictions instead of generating text. When an LLM processes an input, it produces logits , which are raw scores for possible next tokens. We can extract the scores for our predefined answers and apply a mathematical function called softmax to convert them into probabilities. For example, when classifying a product review, the model might produce: Positive: 2.0 (logit) Negative: 1.0 (logit) After applying softmax, we get approximately 73% positive and 27% negative. These probabilities are relative to the options we selected. We can take this further by replacing the usual text-generation layer with a small prediction head and fine-tuning the model on decision-making tasks. This lets it score multiple options, and potentially answer several questions, in a single forward pass. The main advantage is that we skip token-by-token text generation , making repeated decisions faster and more efficient. Open-Source Decision AI Models and Frameworks Jev is a proprietary model available through TypeSafe's API. Although the company has shared some details about its approach, it hasn't published the full architecture, model weights, or training recipe. So we still don't know exactly how everything works under the hood. Meanwhile, the open-source community has been moving incredibly fast, releasing alternatives that we can inspect, fine-tune, and run locally. Some are already reporting better results on specific benchmarks, faster inference, and potentially lower running costs. Here are five projects worth exploring: Laya : A lightweight decision model supporting over 100 languages. It offers fast inference, automatically selects the appropriate model, and runs on modest hardware. Kev : A family of Qwen-based models ranging from 0.8B to 27B parameters. It supports long documents, custom fine-tuning, and deployment through a Jev-compatible API. Simple Jev : Lets us use existing Hugging Face models for classification and scoring without additional training. It also supports vision models for making decisions about images. Decider : Designed to handle multiple decisions in a single forward pass. It supports up to 255 choices per question and includes experimental demonstrations involving games such as Tetris and Pong. SemIf : Focuses on local decision-making, with support for NVIDIA GPUs, Apple Silicon, and CPUs. It includes an interactive browser demo and reproducible benchmarks for comparing accuracy and inference speed. The interesting part is that we now have several ways to build decision-making applications without depending on a closed-source API. We can choose smaller models for speed, fine-tune them for our specific tasks, or run everything locally to reduce API costs. Running Decision AI Locally With llama.cpp Things are moving quickly. Both Ollama and llama.cpp now support decision models through the TypeSafe-compatible /v1/systemone endpoint. Ollama supports models such as Nimble and Tev1, while llama.cpp supports Laya, Kev, Julia-1, and OpenJev. Let's try Laya using the latest llama.cpp. Start the local server: llama update llama serve -hf ggml-org/Laya-GGUF Once the model is running, open another terminal and send a customer support request: curl http://localhost:8080/v1/systemone \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "state": "I was charged twice for my order.", "questions": { "department": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments and refunds", "shipping": "Delivery problems", "technical": "Bugs and account issues" } } } }' The model will evaluate the message and return the selected department along with a probability for each option. That's it. We can now experiment with a decision model locally without using a paid API. The Future of Decision AI I think the most interesting part of Decision AI is how it can work alongside existing LLMs to make AI applications faster and cheaper. Imagine an AI coding agent using a small decision model to select the right tool, decide whether to search the web, or determine if a task needs a more powerful LLM. Instead of using an expensive reasoning model for every little decision, we can reserve it for tasks that actually need it. Another exciting area is real-time applications. Decision models are already being tested in games, where they can choose the next move in milliseconds. We could see similar applications in robotics, fraud detection, and autonomous AI agents. With Ollama and llama.cpp now supporting these models, we can also run them locally, reducing API costs and keeping sensitive data on our own hardware. The biggest challenge is reliability. If a model says it is 95% confident, we need to know whether we can trust that number. Better training, calibration, and human review will be important as these models move into real-world applications. Abid Ali Awan ( @1abidaliawan ) is a certified data scientist professional who loves building machine learning models. Currently, he is focusing on content creation and writing technical blogs on machine learning and data science technologies. Abid holds a Master's degree in technology management and a bachelor's degree in telecommunication engineering.

title: Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth
abstract: research area Computer Vision content type paper published November 2026 Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth Authors Peiyun Hu, Marko Mihajlovic, Lyndon Duong, Lahav Lipson, Wei Dong, Amaël Delaunoy, Stephan R. Richter, Vladlen Koltun View publication View source code (GitHub) Copy Bibtex We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights here . Depth Pro 2 estimates the depth of every pixel, in meters, from images taken with an ordinary camera. One network handles a single photo, a whole video, or a live camera feed, at the input’s full resolution. Its depth is sharp at object edges and steady from frame to frame. Related readings and updates. Sharp Monocular View Synthesis in Less Than a Second December 13, 2025 research area Computer Vision , research area Methods and Algorithms conference ICLR We present SHARP, an approach to photorealistic view synthesis from a single image. Given a single photograph, SHARP regresses the parameters of a 3D Gaussian representation of the depicted scene. This is done in less than a second on a standard GPU via a single feedforward pass through a neural network. The 3D Gaussian representation produced by SHARP can then be rendered in real time, yielding high-resolution photorealistic images for nearby… Read more Depth Pro: Sharp Monocular Metric Depth in Less Than a Second October 9, 2024 research area Computer Vision conference ICLR We present a foundation model for zero-shot metric monocular depth estimation. Our model, Depth Pro, synthesizes high-resolution depth maps with unparalleled sharpness and high-frequency details. The predictions are metric, with absolute scale, without relying on the availability of metadata such as camera intrinsics. And the model is fast, producing a 2.25-megapixel depth map in 0.3 seconds on a standard GPU. These characteristics are enabled by… Read more Discover opportunities in Machine Learning.
