title: Qwen3 TTS is now available on Together AI
Tencent Hy4 is live on Together AI
Interactive Databricks Reference Architectures Across 70 Industries
abstract: Most Databricks architecture talks used to start with the same slide: ingestion on the left, the lakehouse in the middle, BI and AI on the right. The slide is correct, but it doesn't specify where a bank's core banking ledger and SWIFT payment messages go. A hospital wants to know what happens to the HL7 messages from its electronic health record (EHR) system and to its DICOM medical images. A utility asks about smart meter reads and the SCADA data coming off the grid. So people redrew the slide for each industry, and the copies drifted apart. They went out of date with every product release, lived on individual laptops, and there was no way to tell which one was current. The Databricks Reference Architecture simplifies this journey. It's a public, interactive board with a version for each of the 70 industries, updated from the Databricks docs, so it doesn't go stale. Every box opens a panel with what it is, who uses it, and where to learn more. You can also copy any board and change it to fit your own systems. The architecture board covers 70 industries across 11 economic sectors as of November 16th 2026. Click a name to open its board. You'll find the same list in the industry picker at the top of the board. You can search for any industry of interest and interact with it. There is also the Standard Reference Architecture, which is the architecture board with no industry bias. The Databricks Platform in the middle is the same across industries. What changes are the things surrounding it. The sources are the systems that industry actually runs: 964 different ones across the 70 boards as of the release of this blog. They're grouped the way people in that sector talk about them. Like EHR, imaging, and revenue cycle in healthcare, or metering, SCADA, and outage management at a utility. Most source boxes also specify what data they send: whether it's batch or streaming, its shape, how much, and how often. By default, a source shows its type, such as Electronic Health Record (EHR). Switch to Branded to see the vendor products instead. The boards also list the data formats each industry exchanges, 186 in all. They run from FIX and ISO 20022 in finance to HL7 , FHIR and DICOM in healthcare and OPC UA in manufacturing, and each one links to the body that publishes it. The teams carry the names each sector uses, like Treasury and ALM at a bank or Grid Operations at a utility, with 1,538 personas across the 70 boards. The medallion layers use the industry's own terms too. On the banking board, Gold holds net interest margin and liquidity ratios. On the healthcare board, it holds length of stay and patient outcomes. And every board has 10 use cases, 4 Genie Agents, 4 AI/BI Dashboards, and 4 Databricks Apps written for that industry. Here's how six of them compare, from the sources to the Silver layer: Every board opens in Simplified. It shows what you need to read the industry: the first entries in each group, key systems like a bank's core banking system, the use cases with Databricks customer stories, and the core cloud services. Detailed view adds everything else such as CI/CD, monitoring, and operational stores, along with captions, capability tags, and descriptions. Switch views in the toolbar. Shared links and exports follow the view on screen. All 700 use cases say what problem they solve, which team benefits, and how they're built on Databricks, with a link to every product they use. 581 of them link to at least one Databricks customer story and those are listed first. When there's a Databricks Solution Accelerator for a use case the panel links to it so that you can start from working code. Genie Agents work the same way. On the pharmaceuticals board, the Trial Enrollment Agent reads the electronic data capture and clinical trial management systems for the clinical operations team, biopharma leaders, and clinical trial managers. Its panel lists the questions those teams would ask it, such as which sites are under-enrolling this month. Click a team to see the people in it, the use cases they own, and the Databricks products they use, with a line on what each product is for. The panel also builds a learning path for that team from free Databricks Academy courses and certifications, adds the customer stories, demos, and videos that matter to them. The medallion layers link to a deployable data model. Open Silver on the banking board and the panel links to the banking model in the Databricks Industry Data Models, with its tables and columns. We introduced those models in Jumpstart your Data Modeling with Databricks Industry Data Models , and the agent that builds them in Reimagining Data Modeling on the Lakehouse: Introducing Vibe Data Modeling . Source boxes go one level down, into the data itself. The process historian on the manufacturing board collects sensor tags from the production lines. Its panel says who uses that data and how much of it arrives, a continuous stream of 10,000 to 100,000 tags a second. This is the part we use most. Before anyone designs anything, two questions come up: does the product run in the region where we deploy and is it GA or still in preview? Pick a region from the Region menu. The board dims every product that region can't run and a panel opens with the full list for that region. It lists every product and feature that the Databricks docs publish, along with their release stage and whether they're available there. When the docs add a note, such as a feature that processes data outside your geography, the panel shows it too. Each row links to the docs page it came from. The list filters like a spreadsheet. Untick GA in the Stage column and you're left with what's in Public Preview or Beta. You can also sort it, search it, and download it to Excel. The address bar keeps your filters, so you can send someone exactly the view you're looking at. If you only want to clean up the board itself, the Stage menu filters the platform by release stage. Turn off Beta and the previews and everything that isn't GA drops out of the picture. That's handy when you need a GA-only architecture for a review. Both the stages and the regions come from the public Databricks documentation. We refresh them before every change to the board and the board shows the date of the last refresh. Every board works on Azure, AWS, and GCP. Switch the cloud, ingestion tools change with it, and the docs links point to that cloud's documentation. The boards are translated into 16 languages, laid out right-to-left for Arabic and Hebrew and the exports are in the language you're reading. Every industry also has its own share link and preview card. Post the link in Slack, Teams, or LinkedIn and it opens on that industry, with its name on the card. Any board exports as a PowerPoint or PDF deck with a contents page, the board, and a page for each use case, Genie Agent, dashboard, and app. In the PowerPoint, the board slide is built from real shapes so that you can move and relabel the boxes. The board also downloads as a PNG, an animated GIF, interactive HTML, an editable draw.io file, a Visio file, a SVG file, an Excalidraw file, or a YAML file you can edit and import back. If you'd rather start from a description the AI Architecture Assistant finds the closest industry for you. Describe the business or attach a whiteboard photo or a PDF and it builds an editable architecture from that industry's board. It runs as a Databricks App in your own workspace and the repository also includes an MCP server that gives AI agents all 70 architectures. Treat an industry board as a starting point. Every company has its own systems, constraints, and history. A sub-vertical can look quite different from its parent industry. Vendor products change too. If you spot something out of date, tell us through the Feedback button. Open the Databricks Reference Architecture , pick your industry and cloud and click any box. The code and an installer for your own workspace are on GitHub .

title: Why PostgreSQL 19 shipped late
abstract: PostgreSQL 19 is now generally available , and there are some really cool things in it: We walked you through what's new on PostgreSQL 19 here . In this post, we take a step back; as PostgreSQL contributors, we want to share some backstory on how a major release comes together, and some reflections on PostgreSQL 19 and what made this release different. Over the past decade, the timing of PostgreSQL major releases has become very predictable: no earlier than the middle of September, and no later than the middle of October. This year was different: PostgreSQL 19 shipped more than a month after that window closed. So, what happened? To answer that, it helps to know what a normal year looks like. PostgreSQL started in the 1980s as the POSTGRES project at UC Berkeley, and it has been developed in the open since 1996. No single company owns it. A worldwide community of developers builds it, and that community values reliability and predictability. Part of that predictability is the calendar: one major release a year, at about the same time each year. Each release takes 14 to 15 months from the first commits to general availability, and that time splits into two phases: When a feature can't be stabilized in time, the usual practice is to defer it to a future major version and keep the release on schedule. All software contains bugs, and PostgreSQL's code base is large, complex, and old. Our git history – converted from CVS – now reaches back more than 30 years, and the first code was written a decade before that. There's a huge amount of code, and that code contains a huge number of bugs. That's always been true, and it hasn't stopped PostgreSQL from being popular or successful. What's different now is that it's become vastly easier to find those bugs. Fixing them has also gotten easier, but not to the same degree. The change came quickly. Around February 2026, developers started noticing that the latest models were good enough to write real code, that the code going to production wasn't as buggy, and that the models were helping them move faster. Reviewing code and researching security issues used to take a lot of human expertise. With AI, they take much less, and how much AI can discover on its own has gone up sharply. You can see the result in PostgreSQL's quarterly update releases. From August 2023 through November 2025, each one fixed between one and four CVEs. In 2026, that went to 5 in February, 11 in May, and 28 in August. Bug fixes per update release followed the same curve, from roughly 50 to 75 per release to about 140 in August 2026. Not every CVE is equally severe though. Many of the bug fixes are long-tail issues. But the volume is still higher than we’re used to. The commit history shows the same thing. Between April 8th, 2025 and September 25, 2025, there were 1037 commits to PostgreSQL's master branch and 724 commits to REL_18_STABLE. In 2026, during the same date range, there were 1443 commits to the master branch and 1169 commits to REL_19_STABLE. In other words, if you look at the number of commits that went into the master branch only between feature freeze and September 25th, it actually declined slightly from last year to this year, but the number of back-patched commits jumped by more than 60%. The commit history shows the same thing. Between April 8th, 2025 and September 25, 2025, there were 1037 commits to PostgreSQL's master branch and 724 commits to REL_18_STABLE. In 2026, during the same date range, there were 1443 commits to the master branch and 1169 commits to REL_19_STABLE. In other words, if you look at the number of commits that went into the master branch only between feature freeze and September 25th, it actually declined slightly from last year to this year, but the number of back-patched commits jumped by more than 60%. It's possible that some of this jump is the result of committers making more mistakes this year than they did last year, but that’s unlikely. Rather, it seems likely that PostgreSQL committers were about as conservative in 2026 as they were in preceding years, but a lot more of the mistakes they made were quickly found by LLMs. And it isn't just mistakes in the latest release. In the same time period, during 2025, there were 248 commits to REL_17_STABLE, and during 2026, there were 433 commits to REL_18_STABLE. In other words, the number of commits being back-patched not just to the release in progress but also to at least one prior release jumped by more than 74% in a single year. The reason for this is simply that a huge number of people on the Internet are now reporting bugs in PostgreSQL that they found using LLMs, and the PostgreSQL committers have been very busy fixing them. Time that would have gone into reviewing what was going into PostgreSQL 19 went into fixing security issues and other bugs in the back branches instead. A few features that were in progress this cycle weren't ready in time, so the project did what it always does and deferred them to a future release. The fixes kept coming right up to the end. The November 12 update release for the supported branches included so many fixes that the release team put out a second release candidate so PostgreSQL 19 could ship with them. In the end, we got PostgreSQL 19 out the door, a few weeks later than usual, and the delay came directly from the project's concern for quality. The way we all develop software has changed, and the PostgreSQL community is adapting. Nobody knows yet exactly how open source software development will change, but contributors across the PostgreSQL project are working hard to figure it out. LLMs are going to push every PostgreSQL developer, and to some extent every software developer, to raise their game. Every feature we write from now on will be scrutinized by AI, and bugs that would have gone unnoticed forever in an earlier era will now be found, sometimes in a matter of hours. That's a big challenge, and an even bigger opportunity to make PostgreSQL better than it's ever been. We're excited to be part of it. title: PostgreSQL 19 is available on Lakebase
abstract: PostgreSQL 19 reached GA today and it's already available on Lakebase. New major versions often take weeks to reach other managed PostgreSQL services. Instead, we wanted to give access to it to our customers the same day. Several engineers on the Lakebase team are PostgreSQL committers and contributors, and they worked on this release directly, from query plan advice to shared memory, locale handling, and release management. To try it, create a new Lakebase project and select PostgreSQL 19 as the version. PostgreSQL 19 is a practical release. There is no single headline feature that changes what PostgreSQL is. Instead, version 19 goes after operational problems that database teams know well: bloated tables, unstable query plans, replica lag, incomplete statistics, and maintenance work that is hard to run safely in production. The common thread is control. PostgreSQL 19 gives you more ways to step in when the defaults are not enough, without giving up the project's bias toward reliability and predictable behavior. The full list of changes is in the PostgreSQL 19 release notes . PostgreSQL uses multiversion concurrency control, so an UPDATE creates a new row version and a DELETE leaves a dead tuple behind. Routine vacuuming makes that space reusable, but it doesn't necessarily return space to the operating system or restore a useful physical row order. Over time, heavily updated tables can become bloated and poorly clustered. The usual fixes have been VACUUM FULL , CLUSTER , or external tools such as pg_repack . The built-in commands work, but they take an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the whole operation, blocking normal access to the table. PostgreSQL 19 adds REPACK , which reclaims space while normal reads and writes continue during most of the operation. For example, a chat application can rebuild its messages table while clustering rows by conversation and send time using an existing index: REPACK reclaims space like VACUUM FULL ; with USING INDEX , it also physically orders rows like CLUSTER . With CONCURRENTLY , PostgreSQL rebuilds the table while normal reads and writes continue, capturing ongoing changes through logical decoding. It then takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock to apply any remaining captured changes and swap the new table and index files into place. This phase is typically brief but can take longer on a busy table. There are operational constraints. Concurrent repacking creates an additional replication slot for the duration of the operation, so it needs free capacity under max_repack_replication_slots and a table with either a non-deferrable primary key or a suitable index-based replica identity. It also needs temporary disk space for a copy of the table and all its indexes, potentially plus a sort file up to the size of the table. Tables with heavy update and delete traffic face an additional limit: the current upstream PostgreSQL 19 implementation fails if more than about 104 million tuples in the target table are updated or deleted while REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) is running. This counts changes made during the repack, not rows already in the table. Not every relation type is eligible. Long-running transactions can delay the final lock. Concurrent repacking is also not MVCC-safe: after it commits, transactions using snapshots taken before the repack began can see the table as empty. Physical clustering also degrades as later writes arrive. REPACK CONCURRENTLY still needs planning, but it brings into core a job that previously required more downtime or an extension. The PostgreSQL cost-based optimizer uses table statistics and cost estimates to choose an execution plan. Most of the time, that works well. Statistics describe individual tables well, but real datasets often contain relationships that are harder to capture. Imagine that enterprise customers make up 0.1% of customers but generate 30% of orders. Per-table statistics cannot capture that cross-table correlation. With an index on orders.customer_id, the planner may estimate that each enterprise customer has only a few orders and choose a nested loop that repeatedly probes the index. If those customers actually account for 30% of orders, each lookup returns far more rows than expected, and a hash join may be more appropriate. PostgreSQL 19 adds pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice for these situations: These components do not add cross-table statistics or replace the planner. Instead, they let you intervene when an inaccurate estimate produces a poor plan. Consider a query that counts orders from enterprise customers: Here, c is the alias for the filtered customers table. The following advice asks PostgreSQL to place those customers on the inner side of a hash join: When PostgreSQL can apply the advice, EXPLAIN reports feedback similar to: matched means the resulting plan complies with the advice. It does not mean the new plan is necessarily better; you still need to evaluate it against the actual workload. Unlike inline optimizer hints, plan advice lives outside the application’s query text. You can inspect the current plan, test focused advice, and then stash it by query ID. pg_stash_advice is the component that applies stashed advice automatically. Create the extension in each database before using its stash-management functions: Create a stash and associate the tested advice with the query ID reported by EXPLAIN (VERBOSE) . Replace <query_id> with the identifier from your plan: Configure the database to use the stash for new connections: Replace appdb with the name of your database. Treat plan advice as a stabilizer once you've diagnosed the problem. Data distributions change, cached prepared statements may keep using an older plan for a while, and the optimizer is still right more often than it is wrong. When the planner unexpectedly switches a critical query to a worse plan, PostgreSQL 19 gives you a supported way to stabilize it. Autovacuum can now use parallel workers when vacuuming indexes, controlled by autovacuum_max_parallel_workers . A new scoring system prioritizes eligible tables based on how urgently they need vacuuming or analysis. New statistics views expose more of what the server is doing: Query-level diagnostics improve as well. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, IO) reports asynchronous I/O activity, and auto_explain.log_io can include the same information in logged plans. PostgreSQL 19 also reports bytes written for full-page images in pg_stat_wal , EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL) , and vacuum and analyze logs. Together, these make performance investigations less dependent on inference. You can see why maintenance work was prioritized, where asynchronous I/O happened, and how many WAL bytes came from full-page images. Logical replication has become core infrastructure for change data capture, migrations, real-time serving, and ETL pipelines. PostgreSQL 19 closes several long-standing gaps: Sequence synchronization removes an awkward migration edge case, especially during major-version upgrades that use logical replication. Copying table rows without advancing their sequences can leave a promoted subscriber generating values that already exist, causing duplicate-key errors. PostgreSQL copies the initial sequence values when the subscription is created with copy_data = true , the default. Later sequence changes are not streamed continuously, so refresh them immediately before cutover: This updates the sequences already known to the subscription to their current values on the publisher. If the publication has gained new sequences, use ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... REFRESH PUBLICATION to add them and synchronize their values before cutover. Asynchronous read replicas add read capacity without making primary commits wait for them. The tradeoff is replication lag. An application can commit a write on the primary, immediately read from a replica, and not find the row because the replica has not replayed the relevant WAL yet. PostgreSQL 19 adds a direct way to coordinate that handoff.

title: Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button
abstract: Google's flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that's been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely. Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There's an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The "I'm Feeling Lucky" button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone. The search button has obviously been a part of Google's search page forever. However, it wasn't in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
abstract: Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers. The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
abstract: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of AWS access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

title: The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification
abstract: The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been “slop” — meaning low-quality output from a large language model. And with so much code being AI-generated now, avoiding slop has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use formal verification systems , which use mathematical proofs and logic to verify the correctness of software or hardware. With AI’s growing prowess at solving math problems , there’s now a number of AI companies offering formal verification systems. They include Harmonic , Theorem , Axiom Math , and a new entrant called &Truth (pronounced ‘and truth’). In this article we’ll look at some of the approaches these companies are taking. In order to better understand the landscape of formal verification systems, we spoke to one of its leading proponents: Clark Barrett , &Truth’s co-founder and co-CEO. He’s also Corbel Professor (Research) of Computer Science at Stanford and was the co-creator of cvc5 , a popular automated reasoning engine used in formal verification. Without getting too in the weeds, cvc5 is what’s called a “solver” for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) , which Barrett says is widely used in companies like Amazon. For instance, cvc5 is used for specification analysis and test generation in Kiro , Amazon’s agentic development environment. “It's been fun to see my tools go from a good idea in the lab to cvc5 is now called billions of times a day in production pipelines at Amazon,” Barrett told us. Via a 2022 paper about cvc5 co-authored by Clark Barrett. When AI coding agent companies talk about “verifying” their work, it typically means agents running tests, critiquing their own output, or having another AI model judge it. So I asked Barrett how far short of real verification does that fall? “The main difference is really just, how do you know when you're done,” he replied. “So if you're testing, patching, scanning — using all these existing tools — they're quite good. I mean, they find a ton of problems. They raise those issues. But you're never quite sure, did I find all of them [the issues] or is there one more lurking there that my tool can't find?” &Atlas, the first tool of &Truth; it’s “a map of the world’s open-source code, starting with code written in the C programming language.” &Truth builds on Lean , an open-source programming language and proof assistant . The company combines AI with automated reasoning techniques to construct proofs that Lean can check. Lean is a language used by frontier models to solve all manner of supremely difficult math problems . For instance, just this week GPT-6.2 Astra produced what Vals believes is “the first Lean proof of Smoktunowicz’s Gap Theorem.” Vals added that Anthropic also used Lean to formalize Fermat’s Last Theorem, a project of 13 million lines. The latest big math news is a report that Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he used Claude to prove the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and he posted the proof in Lean . Example of Lean code; via Lean project website &Truth is building what it calls a “verification machine” on top of the Lean framework, with the ambition of reading code “in any language, proving whether it satisfies precisely stated requirements , and enabling humans to trust it without having to understand every line.” “What Lean does is it just checks that you didn't make a mistake,” explained Barrett. “So you can think of it as a very sophisticated checker for mathematics.” This has implications for model training too. Axiom Math uses formal verification to provide correctness feedback for training its mathematical reasoning systems, with proof attempts helping improve future models. In an interview with Latent Space in June , Axiom CEO Carina Hong made the point that formal verification — and what Lean enables — isn’t just a defensive measure. “Formal verification, or verified AI, to us it's not just about handling or kicking out the lousiness, the hallucinations, the mistakes. It's about scaling brilliance. It's about super-intelligence.” Axiom develops AxiomProver , an AI system that generates Lean proofs, alongside AXLE , its toolkit for exploring, validating, and manipulating those proofs. Harmonic’s Aristotle , an “ automated theorem prover ”, uses Lean heavily in its offering. “Inside Aristotle, AI writes the proofs and Lean checks every step of them, so a result never rests on the AI being right,” states the company on its website. Given the heightened level of paranoia about cybersecurity these days — some might say in the days leading up to AGI — formal verification systems seem like they’re needed more than ever. And Barrett confirmed that cybersecurity is a key focus for &Truth. “One really powerful use case for our technology is going through all the C code in the world, whether it be open source or closed source, and trying to ensure that it's memory safe. And then if it's not memory safe, we can point to: here's a problem with this piece of code, you need to fix it so that it's safe.” Security is also a focus of Theorem , one of &Truth’s competitors. “Verification is the only defense that holds while adversaries scale,” Theorem states on its homepage. Theorem’s proof-efficiency eval : “KB of machine code verified per hour on our proof-efficiency eval, by model release date, with 95% intervals.” Theorem has also collaborated with Anthropic on this topic, resulting in a blog post entitled “ LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale .” One of the more encouraging notes in the post is that formal verification, although currently token-expensive, is starting to get more token-efficient. On a set of 36 small verification tasks, Anthropic reported that Opus 5.5 reached a 50% solve rate using about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. This trend is expected to continue as more models are “trained on long verification tasks.” Theorem and Anthropic describe “LLM-scaled formal verification” as a promising approach to providing security guarantees at a previously impractical scale. Anthropic diagram: “from code to a machine-checked guarantee”; in this case using Rocq rather than Lean. Lastly, how does formal verification fit into a developer’s workflow? On its website, &Truth states that developers will move from vibe-coding to “veri-coding” — meaning the verification layer is part of the workflow. “If you've got your verification machine connected to your agent, you can still say, ‘hey, I want you to build this,’ said Barrett. “Maybe there's a little bit of work to really nail down with the agent what the specification is of what you want to build. But then the agent can go under the hood, collaborate with the formal [verification] tool, and essentially what you'll see is almost no difference except your code will work the first time.” The idea, then, is that more of the developer’s time will be spent on spec writing and reviewing than on coding or reviewing code. While I was finishing up this article, I came across this tweet by Cognition dev rel Nader Dabit: Whether the term “outcome engineering” sticks or not, he’s onto something in terms of where we are with coding. When you just tell your team of agents what you want and they go ahead and build it, you (the human developer) need a way to check the correctness of what your agents deliver. If companies like &Truth, Harmonic, Theorem and Axiom Math have their way, formal verification could become an increasingly practical way to check those outcomes.

title: [AINews] Anthropic successfully completes largest IPO in history, valued at $1.5T
abstract: As we previewed on our Know Before You IPO pod , Anthropic set its IPO price at $83 and today $ANT closed at $97.17, up 17% from the offering price ( drifting -5% to $92.60 after the close) . The $81.3B offering overtook SpaceX's June IPO as the largest in history. Dario and Daniela ( Dario’s remarks , Founders’ letter ) used the occasion to say Anthropic would pace training and deployment based on whether it could keep its systems safe and under human control. Their Class F shares carry 50.1% of voting power on most shareholder matters. Expect the lockup expiries to weigh on the stock price as about a trillion dollars of shares free up over the next year, while Anthropic has to keep the world’s top model ... for now . AI News for 11/18/2026–11/19/2026. We checked 12 subreddits and 544 accounts on X . Search past issues in the AINews archive . Anthropic listed on Nasdaq under $ANT, priced at $83, and opened 34% higher, putting it near a $2T valuation. Listing: Anthropic rang the Nasdaq opening bell ( @kimmonismus , @yacinelearning ). The official account posted a media-only launch item that drew by far the day's highest engagement ( @AnthropicAI ). Opening trade: $ANT opened at $111.50 , which is $28.50 (34.3%) above the $83 IPO price ( @TheRundownAI , @kimmonismus ). Pre-open indications were up ~32% at ~$110 ( @kimmonismus ). Record raise: The $81.3B raised beats SpaceX's $75B (June) as the largest IPO ever ( @TheRundownAI ). Net proceeds: Expected net proceeds are $104.8B including a concurrent private placement. Fully diluted valuation was ~$2T at the open ( @kimmonismus ). AMD investment: AMD agreed to invest $2.5B in Anthropic alongside the IPO. The same morning, AMD fell after a Hunterbrook report that a US-blacklisted Chinese server maker kept shipping newer AMD firmware ( @kimmonismus , source ). CEO statement: Dario Amodei published IPO remarks with a strong safety commitment (details below) ( @AnthropicAI ). Employee wealth: The average employee could be worth >$40M , per SEC filings and investors ( @kimmonismus ). Anthropic's 5,300 founders and employees are now worth more than the bottom third of US households, about 45M families ( @SteveRattner ). Personal framing: Dario and Daniela lost their father to a disease that became curable a few years later. Dario cited CRISPR's decades-long path from discovery to treatment. Core thesis: Powerful AI working with humans "could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade." He stressed that only early results exist so far. Named risks: Misuse by individuals or nation-states, economic disruption, and loss of control. Listed safety work includes bio/cyber safeguards, alignment training, and interpretability ("like an X-ray"). Key commitment: "We will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business or political pressure." Strategic framing: The IPO "only strengthens our resolve." He restated the "race to the top," which should work "regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time" ( @AnthropicAI ). Low cash burn: Anthropic raised ~$140B and still holds ~$132B on the balance sheet. That implies it "burnt like under $10 billion" to get here, per Tanay Jaipuria (Wing VC) on Latent Space. He called the burn the S-1's biggest surprise, "in a positive way" ( @FounderClipsHQ ). Bear math from FT Unhedged: A 20% return on ~$1T of compute commitments, at a 40% operating margin and 17% tax, requires ~$602B/yr revenue . That exceeds Alphabet ($471B) and Apple ($478B), and equals two-thirds of the $908B earned by all 76 software/IT companies in the S&P 1500 ( @rohanpaul_ai ). Use of proceeds: Proceeds are slated largely for data center leasing, which makes SpaceXSI (the Colossus landlord) an indirect beneficiary ( @kimmonismus ). A critic noted that Elon "rented them an entire Colossus cluster" despite past attacks on Anthropic ( @LinusMixson ). Google's stake: Google owns 13.7% of Anthropic stock ( @NielsRogge ). Teortaxes argued Google could still "fumble this by continuing to reinforce Anthropic with TPUs" ( @teortaxesTex ). After-tax reality check: The median employee likely takes home closer to ~$5M after taxes than the ~$50M headline figures suggest ( @futurenomics ). Product standing on IPO day: Anthropic is #1 lab on Code Arena WebDev, with Claude Fable 5.2 at 1824 , +27 over the next lab ( @arena ). Arena also posted a lineage visual from Opus 4.5 to Opus 5.5 Max ( @arena ). Dustin Moskovitz: The EA funder and major Democratic donor made a critical early bet but is reportedly unhappy, with deep worries about the IPO and fights with Altman, Zuckerberg and Musk ( @teddyschleifer ). The report says Dario and Daniela haven't spoken to him in over a year, and he no longer speaks to Zuckerberg, Altman or Holden Karnofsky ( @teortaxesTex ). Wealth-pledge jokes: Sarcastic takes followed on the giving-away-wealth theme ( @scaling01 ), including "the real winners of the day are factory farmed chickens" ( @shakoistsLog ). Sol Bier (small VC): He credits LPs including GM pension for backing him as an unproven manager. He thanked ICONIQ, Coatue and Lightspeed for backing Anthropic "after the worst stretch in growth investing history" ( @solbier1 ). Former Anthropic researcher Karina Nguyen recalls him as "the only VC I've met who understood scaling laws" ( @karinanguyen ). Aravind Srinivas also vouched for him ( @AravSrinivas ). Other investor posts: General Catalyst framed the company as founded by "seven people... on a contrarian idea: the safest way to build AI is also the best way" ( @generalcatalyst ). Altimeter posted congratulations ( @AltimeterCap ). Sarah Guo nodded to Yasmin Razavi's "victory in total silence" ( @saranormous ). Retail access: On the eve of the IPO, Sarah Guo's No Priors with Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev discussed retail access to private upside ( @saranormous , ep ). Company traits: Founded in 2021, the "first Neolab IPO" is coding-focused, has no image or video models, and "not a single cofounder has left" ( @Yuchenj_UW ). An early Claude was demoed as a Slack bot about 4 years ago ( @iScienceLuvr ). Best business ever: One take called it "by far the best business in the history of capitalism to date," built "while building and deploying AI responsibly" without racing to the bottom ( @MillionInt ). RSI thesis: Anthropic could become more valuable than Alphabet and Meta. Since "only few companies [will reach] RSI," holding ANT makes sense ( @ arohan , @ arohan , @ arohan ). Scaling01 added that "Anthropic is certainly taking off" ( @scaling01 ) and "so fun when the market finally prices in RSI" ( @scaling01 ). He also joked about "a 10% discount for a share of the future lightcone" ( @scaling01 , @scaling01 ). Customer endorsement: Perplexity's CEO said "Opus 5.5 remains the best model in the industry by a good margin" ( @AravSrinivas ). The ad: The IPO ad was widely praised, even by critics. One called it "mind blowingly great" ( @cloneofsimo ). Teortaxes wrote "main character energy... I could see Shockley authorizing this ad" ( @teortaxesTex ). Retail enthusiasm: One user went "all-in" with 2 months' salary ( @stablequan , @stablequan ). Another switched subscriptions to Claude as a new shareholder ( @AishvarR ). Generic congratulations: @c_valenzuelab , @reach_vb , @gojira , @fabianstelzer , @arunv30 , @iScienceLuvr , @tarstarr . Social jokes: Friends joked about the new wealth ( @imjaredz , @imjaredz , @kelin_online , @kimmonismus , @scaling01 , @dejavucoder ). Open science: Clem Delangue hopes $ANT brings "more open science and open-source AI" to "fight concentration of power, capabilities and wealth" ( @ClementDelangue ). Competitors: Aidan Gomez hopes Anthropic "adjusts its strategy to support a healthy community of competitors and a diversity of different ideologies" ( @aidangomez ).

title: Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
abstract: Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work. When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues. Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads. Jump to the "issue tracking is dead" discussion → The thing speeding up purchases right now, Cristina says, is AI budget. Companies carved out money for AI tools that didn't exist before, and any product that fits inside it skips the usual fight for spend. At some companies that budget is very high. It's already starting to change. Buyers are signing one-year deals and paid pilots, not three-year contracts, because nobody knows what they'll want in two years. And some overnight-$100M stories are a handful of $30 to $40 million contracts with defense companies or giant law firms. That's a very different business from Linear's 40,000 paying customers on what was, until June, entirely seat-based pricing. When those one-year deals come up for renewal, we'll find out whose ARR was real. Jump to the AI budget discussion → Three weeks after joining in 2023, Cristina crossed "move upmarket to enterprise" off Linear's company goals. It had one salesperson. She went after growth-stage companies that would have to rip out an existing tool instead, the same way Stripe won new businesses long before it won switchers. Linear finally declared an enterprise push in 2025, with a roadmap full of features for large organizations. Then agents happened. Linear built an MCP server, an agents platform with a whole new set of APIs, and integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot. None of it was planned, and a lot of the enterprise work never got done. Cristina chose to race ahead anyway. Competitors waited, and enterprises started putting Linear on their shortlists. Jump to the enterprise roadmap discussion → Linear has never hired a single SDR. Cristina thinks the qualification call wastes the customer's time: they want a demo, not questions about their budget. AEs do their own outbound, with tooling to keep it personal. It doesn't do forward deployed engineering either. Linear should be easy enough to adopt that nobody needs access to your systems. Solutions engineers sell alongside enterprise AEs instead, sometimes building a working ServiceNow integration overnight to show a prospect it can be done. Cristina adds that an opinionated tool gives agents cleaner data than one where every team defines "bug" differently. Support stays in-house, and Linear won't let an LLM answer tickets on its own. AI drafts replies and a human decides what goes out. Customers sometimes assume the replies are AI because they arrive so fast. In three and a half years, Cristina has never had an escalation over a bad support experience. Jump to the sales team discussion → Cristina would love a model like Intercom's Fin, which charges for each support conversation its AI resolves. It's harder for Linear. What is auto-triaging a bug to the right team worth when one company thinks that's the PM's job and another doesn't? Until someone cracks that, Linear charges for what costs it money and keeps the rest free. Seats stay. Linear Agent chat is free even though it runs on frontier models. In coding sessions, users pick OpenAI or Anthropic models and harnesses, and Linear passes through the published API price plus a small markup. Loops run on AI credits. Linear doesn't start charging for things that used to be free. New AI features launch as free betas with notice that pricing is coming, and prices start high and come down rather than the other way around. Jump to the pricing discussion → Cristina says Linear runs on about half the headcount of companies at its stage and revenue. A sales team bigger than the rest of the company would have cost it the trust engineering now has in sales. From Stripe she brought a 40% rule: at least 40% of the company should be engineering, product, design and data. If sales wanted more people, it helped recruit engineers first. Linear has no hard rule, but one of the first things she built was a headcount spreadsheet by function, and she still watches the ratio. Hiring is slow on purpose. Candidates do a work trial on a real problem. Hers was writing Linear's go-to-market plan for the next six to twelve months, which then became her job. At about 170 people, the only C-suite is the founders and her. Jump to the hiring discussion → Linear — the product development system where Cristina is COO. Sharing Linear's growth with the people building it — the August tender at a $2.5 billion valuation, with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention. Issue tracking is dead — Karri's March post on why Linear is building for agents. Linear MCP server — the May 2025 launch Cristina says was basically a first for the category. Introducing Linear Agent — the built-in agent whose chat Linear keeps free. How we built Triage Intelligence — the feature that suggests labels and catches duplicates in incoming issues, Cristina's example of AI that doesn't need to be an agent Coding sessions in Linear — the June launch that ended Linear's all-seat pricing, running Claude Code and Codex on AI credits. Introducing Loops — recurring agent jobs, also billed with AI credits. Intercom Fin pricing — $0.

Polymarket odds backed by real money and insider information. That's millions of people voting with their attention and their wallets every day. /last30days searches all of it in parallel, scores it by what real people actually engage with, and an AI agent judge synthesizes it into one brief. Google aggregates editors. /last30days searches people. You can't get this search anywhere else because no single AI has access to all of it. Google search doesn't touch Reddit comments or X posts. ChatGPT has a deal with Reddit but can't search X or TikTok. Gemini has YouTube but not Reddit. Claude has none of them natively. Each platform is a walled garden with its own API, its own tokens, its own auth. But you can bring your own keys and browser sessions, and suddenly an AI agent can search all of them at once, score them against each other, and tell you what actually matters. That's the unlock. Not one better search engine. A dozen disconnected platforms, bridged by an agent. /last30days Peter Steinberger You have a meeting tomorrow. You Google them. You get their LinkedIn from 2023. /last30days gives you what they're actually doing this month: joined OpenAI to work on Codex, fighting Anthropic's ban on third-party agents, shipping 23 PRs at 85% merge rate, building "LobsterOS" for cross-device agent control, and r/ClaudeCode hit 569 upvotes debating whether he's a hero or "insufferable." Scattered across X posts, Reddit threads, YouTube transcripts, and GitHub commits. None of it was on Google. Why this exists I built it to keep up in AI. Everything changes every day and the Reddit and X nerds are always on top of it first. I needed better prompts, and the training data was always months behind what the community had already figured out. But it turned into something bigger. Now I run it before a sales call to know the last 30 days truth about a business. Before a meeting to read someone's recent tweets and podcast transcripts. Before a Disney World trip to know which rides are closed and what the community says about Genie+. Before I build anything to know what problems people are actually hitting. If you're meeting with a CEO, have you read all their tweets and YouTube transcripts from the last 30 days? I have. Sources, scored by the people Source What the people tell you Reddit The unfiltered take. Top comments with real upvote counts, free, no API key. The real opinions that Google buries. Free, no API key. Shows when your topic is a listed company or the person who leads one and yahoo-finance-pp-cli is on PATH (first-run setup installs it). LinkedIn The professional signal. Posts and articles, with articles weighted as high signal. Meta Ads What a brand is paying to say. Live Meta ad creatives launched this month, with copy, promo codes, and spoken transcripts. StockTwits Trader sentiment. Auto-activates when your topic is a ticker or crypto. Threads The post-Twitter text layer. Conversations from creators and brands. Pinterest Visual discovery. Pins, saves, and comments on products and ideas. Xiaohongshu (RED) Chinese lifestyle, product, and creator signals. Requested explicitly with --search xhs when a logged-in x-mcp browser plugin or xiaohongshu-mcp service is running locally. Bluesky The decentralized social layer. AT Protocol posts from the post-Twitter migration. Perplexity Controlled Agent API synthesis, OpenRouter Sonar fallback, raw Search API rows, and explicit Deep Research. DEV Community (dev.to) Developer articles and top comments through the public, keyless API. Opt in with --devto-tags , --search devto , or INCLUDE_SOURCES=devto . Truth Social Posts searched with TRUTHSOCIAL_TOKEN ; available when authenticated. Telegram Public posts from named channels. Opt-in; requires SCRAPECREATORS_API_KEY and a channel list. DripStack Financial newsletters and analyst writeups through a public, keyless API. Opt in with --search dripstack or INCLUDE_SOURCES=dripstack . A company run reads it automatically, and roles that hint at something unannounced become Jobs Page Secret Signals. Also selected with --hiring-signals , --search jobs , or the research plan. A filing becomes a Patent Secret Signal only when it is out of character for the company or describes something it has not shipped or announced. Local corpus Your local Markdown and text files, plus PDFs when pdftotext is on PATH. Opt in with --corpus or LAST30DAYS_CORPUS_DIRS . Web The editorial coverage, the blog comparisons. title: appwrite/appwrite
abstract:
Appwrite The open-source cloud for agents and developers. Appwrite is an MCP and agent-first platform for building and scaling apps. Give your agents Auth, Databases, Storage, Functions, Messaging, Realtime, and Hosting, all in one place. English | 簡體中文 Appwrite is an MCP and agent-first, open-source platform for building and scaling apps. MCP is included, so coding agents can operate on a live Appwrite project. Appwrite is available as a managed cloud platform and can also be self-hosted on infrastructure you control. It is designed for the AI agents in your workflow as well as for developers. Connect Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, and other agents through the hosted MCP server, or integrate an SDK into your app. Modular products stay unified from the first prototype to production scale. Find out more at https://appwrite.io . Table of Contents: Products Installation & Setup Self-Hosting Unix Windows CMD PowerShell Docker API version mismatch Upgrade from an Older Version One-Click Setups Getting Started Agents SDKs Client Server Architecture Contributing Security Follow Us License Products Appwrite Auth - Authenticate users securely with email, SMS, OAuth, anonymous sessions, and magic URLs. Appwrite Databases - Model, query, and scale with Appwrite databases or managed PostgreSQL and MySQL, so you can match your use case and team needs. Appwrite Storage - Store files with compression, encryption, image transformations, and access control. Appwrite Functions - Deploy serverless functions with secure isolated runtimes and event-driven execution. Appwrite Sites - Deploy static, SSR, and CSR frontends from Git with instant previews and Appwrite behind them. Appwrite Messaging - Send email, SMS, and push notifications through a unified messaging service. Appwrite Firewall - Protect apps with traffic rules, abuse controls, and edge security for every project. Appwrite Realtime - Subscribe and react to events across your project as they happen. Appwrite MCP - Connect agents to your Appwrite project, APIs, and docs. MCP is included on Cloud, with no local install required. Installation & Setup The easiest way to get started with Appwrite is by signing up for Appwrite Cloud . Cloud includes a Free plan so you can start building immediately, with paid plans when you need to scale. Self-Hosting Appwrite was designed from the ground up with self-hosting in mind. You can install and run Appwrite on any operating system that can run a Docker CLI . Running your server is as easy as running one command from your terminal. Before running the installation command, make sure you have Docker installed on your machine. The setup wizard listens on port 20080 and is published on localhost only. It also prints a one-time installer secret to STDOUT — open the printed URL (or send x-appwrite-installer-secret ) to complete setup. For a remote host, SSH-tunnel to 127.0.0.1:20080 rather than publishing the port on all interfaces. Unix docker run -it --rm \
    --publish 127.0.0.1:20080:20080 \
    --volume /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    --volume " $( pwd ) " /appwrite:/usr/src/code/appwrite:rw \
    --entrypoint= " install " \
    appwrite/appwrite:2.7.2 Windows CMD docker run -it --rm ^ --publish 127.0.0.1:20080:20080 ^ --volume //var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock ^ --volume " %cd% " /appwrite:/usr/src/code/appwrite:rw ^ --entrypoint= " install " ^ appwrite/appwrite:2.7.2 PowerShell docker run - it -- rm ` -- publish 127.0 . 0.1 : 20080 : 20080 ` -- volume / var / run / docker.sock: / var / run / docker.sock ` -- volume ${pwd} / appwrite: / usr / src / code / appwrite:rw ` -- entrypoint = " install " ` appwrite / appwrite: 2.7 . 2 Once the installer is running, open the URL printed in the terminal (it includes a one-time secret) to complete the setup wizard. After installation, go to http://localhost to access the Appwrite console from your browser. Please note that on non-Linux native hosts, the server might take a few minutes to start after completing the installation. Docker API version mismatch If install or upgrade fails with an error like client version 1.52 is too new. Maximum supported API version is 1.42 , the Docker CLI inside the Appwrite image is newer than your host Docker Engine. Pass DOCKER_API_VERSION set to the maximum API version from the error (or upgrade Docker on the host): docker run -it --rm \
    --env DOCKER_API_VERSION=1.42 \
    --publish 127.0.0.1:20080:20080 \
    --volume /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    --volume " $( pwd ) " /appwrite:/usr/src/code/appwrite:rw \
    --entrypoint= " install " \
    appwrite/appwrite:2.7.2 Use the same --env DOCKER_API_VERSION=... flag with --entrypoint="upgrade" when upgrading. For advanced production and custom installation, check out our Docker environment variables docs. You can also use our public docker-compose.yml and .env files to manually set up an environment. Upgrade from an Older Version If you are upgrading your Appwrite server from an older version, you should use the Appwrite migration tool once your setup is completed. For more information regarding this, check out the migration instructions . One-Click Setups In addition to running Appwrite locally, you can launch Appwrite using a pre-configured marketplace app for instant setup. Choose from one of the providers below: DigitalOcean Gitpod Akamai Compute AWS Marketplace For custom deployments on a cloud provider or PaaS, see the guides for AWS , DigitalOcean , Google Cloud , Azure , Coolify , and Dokploy . Getting Started Getting started with Appwrite is as easy as creating a new project, connecting an agent, or integrating an SDK into your code. You can start from a prompt, a quick start tutorial, or the hosted MCP server. Agents Designed for the AI agents in your workflow. Query a database, chart traffic, or ship a change: your agent does it on a live Appwrite project. The hosted MCP server uses OAuth, so you do not need to create or manage API keys. For a self-hosted instance, use the local MCP server instead. Add the remote server to Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, VS Code, and other MCP clients: { "mcpServers" : { "appwrite" : { "url" : " https://mcp.appwrite.io/ " }
    }
} You can also add the MCP server to Cursor in one click. Install language-specific agent skills so models generate correct SDK calls: npx skills add appwrite/agent-skills Browse quick start prompts , generate an AGENTS.md file for your repo, or see the AI tooling docs for IDE and vibe coding setup. Getting started with your platform of choice is also covered in the tutorials below. Platform Technology Web app Quick start for Web Quick start for Next.js Quick start for React Quick start for Vue.js Quick start for Nuxt Quick start for SvelteKit Quick start for Astro Quick start for TanStack Start Quick start for Refine Quick start for Angular Mobile and Native Quick start for React Native Quick start for Flutter Quick start for Apple Quick start for Android Server Quick start for Node.js Quick start for Python Quick start for .NET Quick start for Dart Quick start for Ruby Quick start for Deno Quick start for PHP Quick start for Kotlin Quick start for Swift Quick start for Go Quick start for Rust SDKs Below is a list of currently supported platforms and languages. If you would like to help us add support to your platform of choice, you can go over to our SDK Generator project and view our contribution guide . Client ✅ Web ✅ Flutter ✅ Apple ✅ Android ✅ React Native ✅ Unity Server ✅ Node.js ✅ Python ✅ Dart ✅ PHP ✅ Ruby ✅ .NET ✅ Go ✅ Swift ✅ Kotlin ✅ Rust Looking for more SDKs? - Help us by contributing a pull request to our SDK Generator !

title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI
abstract:
Abstract In our previous post, Redwood , we showed that given an architecture, our AI systems could implement, verify, and deploy an inference accelerator in record time. However, similar to other scientific domains, we believe that AI systems, given the correct freedom and guardrails, can co-design software and hardware together, making optimizations across the stack and opening a design space so large it was previously inaccessible. We set out to answer the question: “Could our AI systems & tools lead to a novel hardware discovery that radically outperforms human-made designs?” Today, we're introducing Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set built from the ground up. Frostbite exploits the properties of interaction nets, namely that every step is local, every dependency is explicit, and every value has exactly one owner, to reach a step-function gain in CPU performance that has long stagnated. On a set of 25 initially chosen workloads, including 15 held out until the final evaluation, we achieved a 4.59x performance-per-watt multiple when compared to a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU core. Our AI systems autonomously iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS. When we took a closer look at the discovered architectural primitives, we were surprised to find novel hardware implementations and runtime features that would have otherwise been difficult to architect. In spite of stagnation in CPU core improvement, we were able to take a workload concept all the way to a final GDS, and prove a step-function increase in perf/W and perf/area. We believe that as AI systems become more capable, every class of chip we know today, from datacenter-grade CPUs, to AI accelerators, to networking switches and NICs, will go through similar fundamental architectural shifts. Introduction to interaction nets Mainstream programming languages, when compiled for general-purpose CPUs, hide the dependencies between the parts of a program. Any piece of code may read or write any variable through a shared, mutable state, and so modern CPU hardware assumes the worst case and rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other. Moreover, single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s, pushing people towards large multicore CPUs such as Intel Xeon, AMD Zen, and NVIDIA Vera. This forces CPUs to maintain the illusion that every core sees the same memory, and keeping that illusion consistent and performant requires deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols that cost area and power, and scale poorly. Interaction nets 1 take a different approach. A program is a graph of nodes, and computation happens by rewriting pairs of nodes that are connected through their ports. Every rewrite only touches a small, local part of the graph. Because each node has exactly one principal port, no two of these active pairs ever overlap, so they can be rewritten in any order, or all at once, and the result is always the same. Interaction nets are also linear: every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state for the hardware to guard. Languages such as Vine 2 compile ordinary-looking programs directly to interaction nets. For an excellent introduction to interaction nets and why they suit hardware, we highly recommend Tendrils' “On Interaction Nets.” 3 Fig. 1. Five queens, two ways. On the left, a C++ program walks the search tree one step at a time. On the right, the same search as an interaction net explores many branches at once: 3,183 interactions with a critical path of only 262 steps. Fig. 1 shows the difference on a small search problem, placing five queens on a five-by-five board. The sequential program visits one candidate at a time. The interaction net exposes all of its independent work: on average, about twelve interactions are ready to run at every step. Nothing about the program was rewritten to get this parallelism; the dependencies were simply never thrown away. In theory, this should have two large advantages. The first is multithreading for free: rather than varying levels of coarse and fine-grained parallelism, parallelism comes straight from the program. No threads, locks, or race conditions, and none of the out-of-order machinery a conventional core uses to dig it back out. The second is that, since every value has one owner and every step is local, data can live in small local memories next to where it is used. That removes much of the area and power a conventional chip spends on large caching subsystems, and much of the system-level complexity of keeping those caches coherent. Process Frostbite was designed with zero architectural priors. We followed the process below, riding multiple agent swarms along the way. Fig. 2. The Frostbite program from first proposal to ablations: key events, the stages of work, and the worktrees the agents created, with each branch drawn in its phase's color. Architecture exploration and selection To begin architectural exploration, we had to establish the set of workloads Frostbite should do exceedingly well in. We decided to look at different ways a program could expose its work: many independent pieces at once, rounds of parallel work, long sequential chains, data-dependent branches, and recursion. Under each category, we created a search set and a held-out eval set to evaluate the final Frostbite on, ensuring the design generalized to programs it was never tuned on. The kernels for FFT, radixsort, and LU follow the implementation in the SPLASH-2 benchmark, although 64 times smaller, because at regular sizes they are not suitable for exploratory work. Later, we added five more practical workloads to the held-out set: a Kalman filter, PCA, finite element analysis, an LU solve, and LZ4 decompression. Fig. 3. All 25 workloads, grouped by how each program exposes its work, and split into the search set the agents tuned on and the held-out eval set, with the size each was run at. Agents synthesized research papers and existing benchmarks, and built Python models to trade off high-level architectural ideas against each other, before narrowing to a single architectural concept. The output of this exploration was a 141-page PDF covering the proposed programming model, the runtime, and the high-level blocks of the chip. This was nowhere near the final architecture, but rather a starting point where all the prior findings, high-level requirements, constraints, experiments, and runtime traits were described. Once the first architectural iteration completed (first RTL generation), this was deleted, since many of the numbers and estimates were well off what was physically possible. Formal contracts and system modeling Once the architecture candidate was selected, our system moved on to building the full software model of the chip. Building software models is essential when exploring an architectural space, as they allow fast iteration between the workloads, the ISA, and the abstracted view of the hardware. Whether we build a CPU, GPU, NPU, or networking switch, mastering this iteration loop allows the fastest exploration of the design space within a finite time. To do this repeatedly, we designed a new in-house specification language, ASL, and wrote Frostbite's system model “Arcmodel” in it. ASL supports machine-checkable translations and refinements between RTL, system models, UVM, SVA, and more, all against a formally backed specification. Its power and performance estimates are accurate to within 1–5%, it runs roughly 200x faster than RTL simulation, and it is formally verifiable through “contracts.” In every silicon program to date, human architects have written many English PDFs before handing off to an implementation team and a verification team.

(600 points, 316 comments on Hacker News)

title: Fuck Your AI Safeguards
abstract:
While refrigerators were getting hacked in Estonia, I half-seriously took a project I’m working on and asked Claude Code if there are any low-hanging fruit regarding
security that we could improve. It found one issue that was easy to fix, simple oversight with a one line fix, so I just
went along with it. Then it got stopped because of bullshit “AI safeguards”. Oh no, how dare I , the senior product engineer with my product that I provably have control over, try to fix and prevent security issues and ensure compliance
with local laws and regulations? “Oh but you can just apply to get an exemption from them here bla bla fucking blah ” Have you READ the requirements? First of all, you will have to wait for multiple business days to get a response. You forfeit any data retention exemptions, so hope you don’t have any IP to protect! Oh, and oh so please give us your fucking ID or passport! We won’t leak it later, promise! WHAT. And you may just get fucked anyway and not get approval. Approval to appropriately protect your own service! This wasn’t the first time I ran into this issue. As maddening as it sounds, I try to keep up with the security
landscape and to apply appropriate mitigations because leaking sensitive information is a big fucking no-no and I
can’t let that happen. If there’s a popular exploit out there that applies for our technical stack, I need to know if the public
proof-of-concept snippets can be adapted and used maliciously against my services. But no, Claude will tell you to fuck
off and use an older model that still will try to stop you from applying adequate protection. You know who don’t need to ask for approval? Criminals. They just go and use the models that don’t have safeguards in
place. Abliterated open weights models don’t care. Bad actors reach their goals with or without your “safe” models. You can use a knife to cut up some food, or seriously hurt someone. Yet I don’t get asked to put in an application with
my government-provided ID to buy one. Why is this tool so special? Predictably, the only way to actually make our own service more secure ended up involving the use of EU-hosted
open weights models, such as GLM 5.3, that actually complied with our intentions, proved that the issue is there, and
then helped fix and verify that the issue is now resolved, for good. Congratulations, Anthropic, you’ve made the world an unsafer place. Or maybe that was your plan all along to get regulators to react and build that moat for you right before your IPO to
fend off competitors? Either way, I’m just incredibly frustrated. Big AI labs use the same tools without restrictions to make the security
landscape a fucking mess, and then they go and prohibit others from using the same tools to protect themselves from the
threats they just created. Fucking asshats. 1 and that’s my swear word quota hit for the year. ↩︎
