title: AI isn't replacing your job. It's turning it into low-paid gig work
abstract:
The gig economy has arrived for cardiologists. Recruiting platform Outlier, run by Scale AI, advertises offers of up to $180 an hour for physicians in the U.S. to design complex cardiac scenarios, review artificial intelligence-generated reports, and rank model outputs. The site offers up to $7.50 an hour for Tagalog work in the Philippines for the same job, and up to $12.50 an hour for Swahili in Tanzania. Companies like Scale AI first outsourced data work to wherever labor was cheapest. Now, they are recruiting physicians, lawyers , and Ph.D.s to generate and annotate data, rank model answers, and verify outputs. Higher credentials can raise the advertised rate, but the platform still controls payment and working conditions. They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on. I’ve spent the last six years interviewing the people who do this work. Most were in Venezuela, where economic collapse has left a large, educated population online and out of options. One of them, Rogelio, taught computer science until the economic crisis and the pandemic left his family without work. His 13-year-old son discovered they could earn money labeling images of cars and roads on the platforms Hive and Scale AI’s Remotasks, using a laptop the Hugo Chávez government had issued to schoolchildren a decade earlier. The boy made 18 cents for a few hours of work. Rogelio joined him and made just over $2 on his first day. For a while, the work paid. A task called Beast Mode where workers labeled objects in people’s homes paid more than any other work the family had done. In December 2020, with schools closed and the whole family working, it brought in $20 in a single day. It was the most they would ever make. By early 2021, Beast Mode had disappeared, and their earnings fell below Hive’s $5 weekly payout threshold. This is how many platforms operate: They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on . Remotasks ended its hourly program in Venezuela in 2021 and made a splash in Kenya the same year. In March 2024, it discontinued operations in Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan. Scale AI attributed the closures to “enhanced security protocols,” and said notices had gone out three weeks ahead but later acknowledged that Kenyan workers never received them “due to operational errors.” Most workers who spoke to Rest of World at the time said the platform simply froze them out. The pattern has a name, and it’s older than AI: extractivism. It is a system that takes resources and value from people and places for accumulation elsewhere, on terms set by the buyer rather than the worker. The term also stands for what is taken and what is left behind. The crisis that put Rogelio’s family online was the residue of an oil economy that built little else. An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else. One woman I interviewed in Venezuela drew a pension from the state oil company. By 2021, it was worth about $1 a month, which she said couldn’t buy half a dozen eggs. She was labeling data on Hive to make up the difference, but that income was even less secure. An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else. AI is usually described as built on extracted data: authors’ books , artists’ works , all used to train models. But the extraction has another layer: the new examples, evaluations, and corrections commissioned to improve those models. That material has to be created by someone, for a fee, which is set by the platform — whether it is $2 for the teacher in Venezuela or up to $180 an hour for a cardiologist in the U.S. Outlier’s terms let the company delay or suspend payment during an investigation of a worker’s tasks and withhold “some or all amounts accrued” where it finds a violation “in the company’s sole determination.” The company may also deactivate an account “immediately without prior notice for any reason.” The same language appeared word for word in the Remotasks terms that Rogelio’s family worked under in 2021. Earlier this year, Josh Dzieza reported on the laid-off lawyers , scientists , and screenwriters now filling these platforms. Of the more than 30 workers he interviewed, nearly all described the same arc: Demands increased, target times shrank, and pay fell as a project went on. One designer was tagging videos for Meta at $21 an hour when the project ended for “scope changes.” Days later, the same job reappeared under a new name at $16 an hour — the same sequence that Rogelio’s family went through five years earlier. Of course, workers can leave, and many do. But the ones who stay are often those who can’t leave. One woman I interviewed was confined to her home during the Covid-19 pandemic by a health condition and couldn’t risk losing the job. “This is my only source of income,” she told me. The rate can change suddenly, the task can disappear without warning, and they have no say over any of it. None of this is unknown within the industry. In a 2024 meeting convened by the nonprofit Partnership on AI and the Fairwork project which rates platform companies, I sat with representatives of AI companies and the outsourcing firms that supply them. The AI companies said they didn’t employ the data workers; the outsourcing firms said their operations were determined by the prices the AI companies expected. Everyone agreed pay should be better, but when the question of representation came up, the room went quiet as no workers were present. Workers have still acted. In March 2023, a judge in Kenya temporarily halted the dismissal of 260 Facebook content moderators, prevented Meta from moving their work to another contractor, and barred Meta and contractor Majorel from blacklisting workers. As workers fought in Kenya, Meta moved the work to West Africa. American courts are also grappling with this issue. Claims by workers on Scale AI’s platforms led to a proposed settlement that has received preliminary approval in San Francisco. The company denies wrongdoing. A separate class action suit alleges Mercor misclassified more than 30,000 lawyers, doctors, and engineers while setting their pay and reviewing their work. Mercor’s clients have included OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, but they are not named as defendants. The case is ongoing. A cardiologist who is offered a three-digit hourly rate is not in the same position as Rogelio and his family. What connects them is the fact that the rate can change suddenly, the task can disappear without warning, and they have no say over any of it. The work will keep moving, and the rules will continue to be set by the companies that commission it, wherever the next worker logs on, whether in Kenya, Venezuela, or the Philippines.

Chrome AI Features Wasting Much Bandwidth ♦ Posted by Jeff Starr in Tech Updated November 20, 2026 • Leave a comment 🔎 Finally solved the mystery . At some point this year (around a few months ago), my bandwidth/data usage went thru the roof. Figured out it was Chrome’s recent AI features. Then got immediate bandwidth-relief after disabling all the “AI innovations” and “On-device” stuff. Here is a screenshot of the settings: Find the Chrome AI settings under “AI innovations” I simply disabled everything on that settings page, and the needless bandwidth leakage stopped immediately . Don’t take my word for it. Fire up your favorite activity/network monitor. Watch the network activity while Chrome’s AI features are enabled, which they are by default . Note the continual bandwidth/data spend coming from Chrome, which if you care to monitor long-term adds up to many GB s per month (depending on setup, usage, etc.). After watching the meter spin for a while, go into the Chrome settings and disable all the “AI innovations” and “On-device” stuff. Then return to the network monitor and watch it virtually flatline. Problem solved . Commentary Chrome should have left the AI resource hogs disabled by default. Someone do the math on how much energy and bandwidth is absolutely wasted by all the people (such as myself) who never touch the AI stuff . Before I disabled the AI settings, Chrome was gobbling endless GB s. Multiply by the number of Chrome users who aren’t using “AI whatever neat”, and you’re talking real numbers. Real waste . title: Court: 4th Amendment Disallows Use Of AI-Generated 'Probable Cause'
abstract:
I don’t know where this decision will take us, but its implications reach much further than the single case it covers. AI is pretty much everywhere, and if a court says an algorithm can’t make probable cause determinations, it affects/infects everything from facial recognition tech to predictive policing software to Axon adding AI shovelware to its omnipresent body cameras under the (correct) assumption cops don’t like writing reports. In this case, Alain Osorio was arrested for allegedly passing a bad check at local bank. The only pictures of the suspect came from the bank’s CCTV footage. This was handed over to Detective Ryan Kilmer of the Florence (KY) Police Department. The detective decided to run a screenshot of the suspect’s face (derived from the CCTV footage) through the PD’s facial recognition program. The decision [PDF] doesn’t specify which facial recognition program was used, but given that the match was made using photos found on Facebook, it suggests Clearview AI might have been involved, given its scraping of hundreds of billions of images from the open web since its inception. Not that it did anything useful in terms of actual detective work. Nor did it do anything remotely constitutional, not when the operative word in “probable cause” is “probable.” Relying solely on the AI identification, Detective Kilmer concluded that the match was accurate. [Id. at 4–5]. The Facebook profile belonged to an individual known as “Yony Smith Npoles Charon,” and for an unknown reason, Detective Kilmer concluded that “Yony” was actually Alain Vizcay Osorio—the man in the booking photo. The court says “for an unknown reason.” I can make an educated guess, however. Passing a bad check is the sort of crime most cops won’t really dig into. Detective Kilmer was handed the case and did the bare minimum: he ran an AI-assisted search. He didn’t actually do anything that resembled actual detective work. But he still felt his 30 seconds of non-existent effort were enough to support a criminal complaint and the issuance of an arrest warrant. Osorio — who lived in Nebraska — was arrested and extradited to Kentucky to face criminal charges. He was released on bond the day after his arrest (January 24, 2025). He was then indicted by a grand jury in March 2025 and arraigned roughly two months later. Again, Osorio pleaded not guilty. At that point, the state’s attorney’s office dismissed the charges after Osorio provided proof he had been working in Nebraska at the time the bad check was being passed by (the presumably still at-large) suspect captured by the bank’s security camera. The only thing the AI used by the detective seemed to be capable of doing was reinforcing the investigator’s “all Black people look the same” prejudices. (To be clear, I don’t specifically know if this detective has these prejudices, but the chain of events in this case certainly support an assumption of this person’s assumptions, if you catch my drift.) The individuals in the security footage and the Facebook profile image do not resemble the booking photo of Osorio. [Id. at 6–7]. Based on the booking photo, the only thing Osorio has in common with the suspect is that he is a black male with facial hair. [Dkt. 3-1 at 2–3]. Based on the photographs, it appears that Osorio has a different head shape, different haircut, different facial features, and different complexion . Detective Kilmer told the court (via his affidavit) that he had used “investigative tools” to “match” Osario to the suspect. In reality, the court says, Kilmer only used a single tool and rolled with its obviously faulty conclusions despite Florence PD policy specifically stating facial recognition AI alone is not enough to “establish probable cause.” Kilmer runs directly into this policy and the Fourth Amendment itself, which poses multiple problems for his desire to walk away fiscally intact from this lawsuit. The policy is undeniable, which means Kilmer deliberately ignored his “training” and any “expertise” it was supposed to impart. But beyond that, there’s the Fourth Amendment itself, which can’t as easily be ignored as cop shop software clickwrap. That much is made perfectly clear in the court’s introductory paragraph: The Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution does not allow a detective to delegate to AI the task of assessing probable cause. In other words, the Fourth Amendment does not permit an individual to be arrested based on nothing more than an uncorroborated conclusion by AI that the individual in question has committed a crime. And no reasonable detective in the Defendant’s position could conclude otherwise. The first part of that suggests implications far beyond this case, given how often “detectives” are letting their fingers do the walking (so to speak) and pretending whatever the computer coughs up is arrest-worthy. That’s not just the facial recognition tech used in this case. This is also the AI that steers patrols and public interactions via so-called “predictive policing.” That’s also the AI that writes reports for police officers, allowing the computer to create the permanent, official record of stops, arrests, and uses of force. But what’s also important is the last sentence of that paragraph. That’s the thing that’s going to make this stick. The detective isn’t shielded by qualified immunity, which means this is sure to be appealed. But if this officer does this (rather than “allow” the people who he’s supposed to be serving to buy him out of a lawsuit via a settlement), he’s going to make this an appellate case. And there’s definitely no reason to assume the higher court is just going to blow off the obvious concerns raised by this lawsuit and allow QI to cover up this compendium of wrongs. For now, the decision stands as it is: AI isn’t probable cause. Never has been. Never should be. And if this court has anything to say about it, it never will be. Detectives who prefer to let computers do their thinking for them might want to dial back their reliance on algorithms. Justice should never be subject to available processing power. And if you lack the desire (or intelligence!) to do detective work properly, well… Filed Under: 4th amendment , ai , facial recognition , facial recognition tech , false positives , florence pd , kentucky , mass surveillance , probable cause A weekly news podcast from Mike Masnick & Ben Whitelaw This feature is only available to registered users. title: AI came for the coders. Understanding why tells us who's next
abstract:
I used to joke that I got my degree in poetry instead of computer engineering so that, in case this computing fad went south, I would have something to fall back on. Thanks to AI, it’s barely a joke anymore. Software engineering, where I’ve spent a good part of the last 25 years of my career, is undergoing a crisis of faith. True believers in the beauty of hand-written code have had it wrested from them. Those who like solving problems and making things with technology, code or no, have been given new toys to play with and tools to master. I liken it to carpentry from the 19th century onward, when jack planes, chisels and hand saws gave way to power sanders, routers, and table saws. The industry scaled, and now ordinary people can afford decent furniture. But there was another cost. The straightforward nature of physical automation If you were happy to become a machine operator instead of a craftsman, you were in business. However, if you fell in love with thin ribbons of wood from a hand plane catching the light, about the only remaining way to make a living now is by filming your craft and becoming an influencer for nostalgic hobbyists. We embraced the automation of manual labour as it led to benefits for many, in affordable goods and free time. We devalued craftsmanship in the bargain. Working at a desk became more respected than making a desk. But when the work of smart coders gets rocked this hard, fear ripples through the desk worker world. If such intellectual work is vulnerable, then what, and who, is next? A comforting but wrong answer is that the “human” stuff is safe, and coding is technical. A much better way to understand what human skills will endure AI automation is to look at a principle as old as machine learning, and one that goes a long way toward explaining what can and cannot be automated by AI. It hasn’t changed since the 50s, and is unlikely to be broken anytime soon. It is easy enough to understand, yet what it predicts can be counterintuitive. So many wrong assumptions, and so much baseless fear-mongering, stem from misunderstanding the nature of AI automation’s natural trajectory. The counterintuitive nature of digital automation In aid of my language studies, I recently created a clone of my voice to help with pronunciation. It took a few hours and about $5 of computing credits to retrain a free open-source model, which now runs locally on my MacBook, entirely within my control. I used it to record one of my AI explainer videos, and played it for my wife, a professional musician with a great sensitivity to voice, who has lived with me for nearly 25 years. She couldn’t tell it wasn’t me. Making art, writing poems and songs, and recognising the face or voice of a loved one feel like inherently human activities. Some of it, like facial recognition, has gone the way computer scientist Larry Tesler predicted: “Intelligence is whatever machines haven’t done yet”. The term “intelligent” didn’t stick to it for long. It has just become a part of everyday life. The ones that feel most like “us”, though, such as art, writing, speaking, and even code, have shaken our sense of identity when done by a machine. Here the AI label stuck fast. Machines doing work we identify with causes us to project our self-image of intelligence onto them as well. Yet AI can also appear incredibly dumb. Researchers who study AI at work have a name for the lopsided progress of AI across disciplines: the jagged frontier. 1 It turns out the line between what the machines do well and what they do badly runs nowhere near the line between what we find hard and what we find easy. The frontier only looks ragged because we are measuring it by how “human” the work feels, which means some disciplines and even industries won’t “just catch up” to the outer edge anytime soon. The truth is, speech synthesis and everything else we either take for granted or fear will bring about our obsolescence all conform to the laws of what AI can automate well. These are rules that follow from how machines “learn”, which is also a purely anthropomorphic metaphor. Understanding what can be automated The first AI programmes of the 1950s were specified with rules of reasoning written by hand. The ones that learned arrived in the same decade, among them a programme at IBM that improved at draughts by playing against earlier versions of itself. 2 Learning needs something more than just design; it needs a way to keep score. This is why AI plays games so well, eventually surpassing us in finding the best way to win. AI researcher Jason Wei coined “verifier’s law”: the easier a task is to check, the easier it is to train AI to do it. Andrej Karpathy distinguishes the old way of doing software as what you can specify and the new way as what you can verify. 3 A digital recording of a voice, it turns out, is easy to check, and easy to verify against the reference voice being cloned. For simplicity, I have bundled all of the elements that Wei and others have identified as necessary for checking and verifying, such as having a right answer, being able to score it reliably, and being able to automate it with sufficient computing power to do it over and over again at high speed, into the term “grading”. All components are necessary to perform AI automation today. But even as data and computing power become more available, at the end of the day some numerical form of analysis, and some evaluation of “correctness”, are make-or-break factors in what can (ever) be graded. Grading, however, is only part of what predicts AI automation. The other part is value, and our agreement on what valuable means. Plotting work along these two dimensions gives us four boxes to consider. Software is among the most-graded work humans have ever produced. It compiles or it doesn’t, the tests pass or they fail, and the automated testing takes seconds on ordinary machines. As long as it’s fit for purpose, nobody disputes that working software is worth having, which puts code in the top-right box. My cloned voice sits beside it. It either passes the wife test or it doesn’t. Yet, as I have said before , there will never be a compiler that can check for bugs in your poem. You can clone a poet’s style, and follow all conventions of form just right. But poetry’s greatest trick is evading mediocrity, which is precisely what endless iterations of numerical comparison and adjustment converge upon. Form and style can be graded; whether the poem is any good cannot. That puts poetry in the bottom-right box. I did a whole talk on it, if you want to hear more. From the standpoint of society, parenting is perhaps the most important job in the world. Grading it automatically (or at all) seems absurd, not least of all because it can take years, even generations, to see the results, which are themselves often easy to recognise but hard to quantify. It sits top left, high in value but beyond grading. The last box holds work that can be neither graded nor valuated objectively. Our carpenters who became hobbyist woodworkers got put in this box by the physical machinery of automation, yet now remain immune to digital automation as a result. Like poetry, the value of the product is a matter of taste, and taste diverges, eluding quantification. Predicting what will be automated Beyond coding, the automation of art and writing feels like the solution to a “problem” that almost nobody wanted to be solved. 4 So much of what has been automated most of us lament, and so much of what has not been automated we begrudge. This is because the possibilities of AI automation do not follow our wishes, but follow the principles of automated grading versus objective value outlined above. It also doesn’t matter how “human” it feels: if it scores high on both, it’s possible. This doesn’t make it probable, however. It just shows us where to rule out the impossible. What makes it probable is market incentive.

title: No Bailout for the AI Bubble, Anthropic IPO Protesters Say
abstract:
News No Bailout for the AI Bubble, Anthropic IPO Protesters Say Justin Hendrix / Nov 19, 2026 Demonstrators used the occasion of Anthropic’s stock market debut to raise various concerns about AI outside the Nasdaq in New York City’s Times Square on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo: Melissa Bender) Republish Share On Thursday, Anthropic executives were at Nasdaq in New York City’s Times Square for the opening bell. The company’s initial public offering (IPO) saw it price shares at $83, and initial demand appears strong before the stock starts trading at midday . But while CEO Dario Amodei and his team of executives — all of whom are set to “ reap fortunes ” today — were all smiles as they applauded the listing, outside Nasdaq a group of demonstrators had rather different expressions. Affiliated with groups including Stop Funding Billionaires , Climate Defiance , Sunrise NYC , Act Up NYC , NYC-DSA , JVP-NYC , Climate Defenders , Planet Over Profit and New York Communities for Change , the demonstrators held signs that read “Stop Tech Oligarchs” and “Freeze AI” as the stock ticker raced by on screens behind them. Representatives of the group used a small, hot-pink megaphone to address the media and onlookers. Between speeches, they chanted slogans such as “Hey, hey. Ho-ho. This IPO has got to go!” and “Anthropic, get off it, put people over profit!” Their concerns ranged from the potential economic impact if the AI bubble bursts to AI’s effects on the environment, healthcare, surveillance, and jobs. Demonstrators protest the Anthropic initial public offering outside the Nasdaq in New York City’s Times Square on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo: Melissa Bender) “We're here because Anthropic poses a threat to us, not Terminator-Skynet-style, even though that might be true, but pension fund-style, because AI is a bubble, and it's a worse bubble than 2008 with the real estate crisis,” said James Inniss, an organizers with New York Communities for Change. “And if our pension funds are the ones that are going to be stripped in five, 10 years when this bubble bursts, we are the ones that have to be out here to fight and tell everybody that that is not acceptable, that is not okay, and we are not standing for that,” he said. Bryce Rogers, an organizer with a group called Resisting Automated Disempowerment (RAD), said he was there to protest the fact that the IPO was moving ahead despite a lack of information about the risks the company’s technology poses. He said he’d read the auditing firm METR’s recent report on Anthropic, but was left with more questions than answers. “All these years that I've been storyboarding the upcoming chapters of my life, these oligarchs have been at the negotiation table with the publishing company,” said Rogers. “It's just been moving so much faster than I foresaw and faster than our government has been able to maturely react.” He praised New York’s Responsible AI Safety and Education ( RAISE ) Act, and called for more organizing to demand greater regulation and transparency. “We can reclaim authorship of our future,” he said. Sommer Omar, an organizer with New York Communities for Change, speaks outside the Nasdaq in New York City’s Times Square on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo: Melissa Bender) ACT UP New York’s Brandon Cuicchi said he was concerned about AI’s impact on healthcare. “What we are seeing around the country already in healthcare is horrifying,” said Cuicchi. “We have hospitals that are cutting staff and trying to replace it with AI. We have medical offices that are trying to pre-screen people. Instead of having a live professional, they will try to screen you with AI. We have AI deciding medical outcomes and treatments in this country. Shame. Shame.” Kenny Moll, an activist affiliated with a campaign called QuitGPT and the Sunrise Movement, said he was concerned about the environmental impact of AI, but also about the relationship between AI firms, surveillance, and the government. “These companies are working hand in hand with fascist governments. We cannot allow this,” he said. Aber Kawas, a Palestinian-American democratic socialist recently elected as a New York State Senator, said AI companies are among the biggest enemies of the progressive movement. “People across this nation are trying to turn the tide to create a country to have their state, their city invest in communities during an affordability crisis, and not in war and destruction,” said Kawas. “And the biggest enemies to that are AI companies and corporate interests, which drive our government to invest in things like AI companies which are destroying our climate, destroying people's lives,” she said. A demonstrator is led away by police with their hands bound AI outside the Nasdaq in New York City’s Times Square on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo: Melissa Bender) There were arrests. One demonstrator in a Greenpeace T-shirt was led away by police after seating themselves with a sign at the entrance to Nasdaq. In a statement following the demonstration, organizers attributed a quote to one of the demonstrators that was arrested. “Our demand is clear: freeze reckless AI development and don’t bail out Big Tech when their bubble inevitably pops,” they said. title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
abstract: Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook ( https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook  and onlook.com). Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community. Here’s a demo video: ( https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM ) If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild. We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do. More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state). Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024:  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862 , August 2024:  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449 , May 2025:  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653 ). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code. How it works… Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal. When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas. The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant. Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is. This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt. We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built. The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams. We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We’re so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code! The Onlook team (Joel - thebrubaker and Kris - krisodd), and I will be here all day!

title: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it
abstract:
Whatever skill you’re learning, it won’t take long before someone with experience in that particular field tells you to get your hands dirty. It’s fine to read “Born to Run”, but you won’t be running an ultra marathon any time soon if you don’t start running. Whether it’s muscle memory, technique, physical fitness or problem solving you need to work on to reach your goals, you need to practice . This isn’t a controversial statement in any field at all , and has never really been. Except in software engineering, somehow. When it comes to software engineering, we somehow lost our way, thinking that our skills won’t stop improving if we stop practicing . Making such a claim in any other field would be sneered at at best. Imagine John Scofield 1 saying he stopped practicing his guitar because “he was at a good enough level, musically, to maintain (and even improve!) his expertise” simply by 1) instructing others on how to play (either in vibe general terms, or with a strict spec musical notation), and then 2) listening to what they played and iterating until it sounded good enough for his next record. “My music is better”, he would claim, and moreover “actually playing the guitar was never the point anyway, there’s more to making music.” Mind you, my point in this post is not to discuss the short term quality of code output (or recorded guitar playing, to continue the proverbial thread), but rather the skill of the craftsman practicing his craft vs the one who doesn’t practice at all. To make another comparison that’s arguably closer to software engineering, or at least the “writing and reasoning about code” part of it, let’s look at authors in other fields. I have no doubt that reading great prose has the potential to nudge a writer towards better writing of his/her own; in fact it’s super important to have creative references to draw upon - no doubt at all. But, imagine an author who 1) stopped writing, and only pursued reading and giving feedback to other writers, and worse yet 2) mostly read AI generated prose !? To be perfectly honest, I would expect a quite steady (if not exponential) decline of this author’s writing skills. “There’s more to software engineering than writing code” Link to heading Sure. But if we can at least agree that the code that runs our software is a non-trivial part of it (though, granted, not all of it by far: The other parts of developing and maintaining software speak even louder against using generative AI as a significant tool service! ), we should aspire to be proficient in understanding how code works, what good code looks like, what to watch out for and how software architecture plays a vital part in making code Easy To Change. Simply “reviewing all the code Claude produced” won’t quite cut it. And who are you trying to fool, after all; at this point you’re not really reading half of it, are you? So I propose something that used to be a no-brainer: Keep practicing! Which brings me to my next point: All engineers(!) need to be good at solving problems Link to heading if || while you can argue that the need for being hands-on on your software’s code varies, I propose you can’t argue that we’re still solving problems . And the moment you stop practicing solving problems is the moment you stop getting better at it, just like everything else. Simple as that. This is hardly new, btw: you could always tell who beat Doom using cheat codes and who finished the game the real way! If the end goal is to “beat the game”, then by all means cheat; if the end goal is getting good at it , then I’d advice you not to. Some lessons are only learned the hard way (trial and error ), and very few are learned without effort at all . Repeated LLM usage for problem solving pounds the following premise into our brain’s wiring: If something is hard, tricky or requires effort, you shouldn’t even try. And right there goes our learning, craft and joy, right out the window. In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy , I don’t want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline , I can’t help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea . It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all? — Em’s blog 2 , emphasis mine. Please, John Scofield, don’t stop playing your guitar! ↩︎ I’m not sure who Em is, but their blog is great! ↩︎

title: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8)
abstract:
Conversation nmouha commented Nov 10, 2026 Copy link Copy Markdown Contributor This fixes "Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()" ( CVE-2026-121481 ) by returning -1 for invalid inputs to EVP_EncodeBlock() : NULL input or output buffers, negative lengths, and lengths for which the encoded size does not fit in an int . The OpenSSL SRT has asked for it to be fixed publicly; the advisory is still pending. Returning -1 for invalid inputs is the most straightforward fix, and matches what happens in wolfSSL's compatibility layer for OpenSSL's EVP_EncodeBlock() . I'm suggesting a similar guard for EVP_DecodeBlock() . No length limit is needed here because the decoded length always fits in an int , but it is a good idea to reject NULL buffers and negative lengths. Moreover, I propose to fix the incorrect length check in the base64encode() function of http_client.c , which rejected only len > INT_MAX . I am adding tests in test/base64_dec_avx2_test.c to cover the new behavior, and documenting the -1 returns in doc/man3/EVP_EncodeInit.pod . Exploiting this vulnerability from the command line is possible by passing a large -proxy_pass to openssl s_client . I confirmed that GOST accepts these large passwords out of the box. However, the password has to be supplied through an environment variable ( env:VAR ), otherwise the command line will be too long. Note: the pattern of CVE-2026-121481 is similar to that of CVE-2021-23840 . title: Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations
abstract:
Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations This repository holds the paper Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations by L. Alpöge and
T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it. Contents paper/finite-time-blow-up-navier-stokes.pdf : the paper (79 pages, version of 20 November 2026). lean/ : the Lean package (Lean v4.33.1 with Mathlib, at the revision pinned in lean/lakefile.toml ). lean/README.md explains how the formal statements relate to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2
and Appendix B of the paper, and where the formal proofs differ from the proofs of the paper. lean/NOTICE says in words what each statement file contains and what is proved. The Lean package The statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in
place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/ . Each comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean , names the theorems whose statements must agree,
and permits only the axioms propext , Quot.sound and Classical.choice . To build, from lean/ : lake exe cache get lake build The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and
time. What is and is not here The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the
paper says that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by
a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through
FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either. The source of the paper is not in this repository. State of the Lean text The package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the
cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes $(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$ , one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics
of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the
conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled.

title: What Comes After AGI?
abstract:
For decades, AI research has been focused on a monumental milestone: building artificial general intelligence, or AGI - machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks. It was always clear that, in principle, intelligence could progress beyond human level, but the prospect of AGI was far enough off, and surrounded by ample uncertainties of its own, that looking past it felt premature. Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next. While far from certain, AI could continue to advance at its current pace - and possibly even accelerate - towards artificial general superintelligence, or ASI. It could have a profound impact on science, the economy, and society at a scale and speed much greater than AGI itself. Preparing for that potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress. The continuum of general intelligence To examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence , whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum. Human-level AGI is just one point along that spectrum. ASI sits further along as an advanced system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years to complete, using fewer resources and less time. Examples would be making the same scientific progress as an entire research field in a fraction of the time, or achieving technological developments, such as in chip design, on par with what large companies can do in a year. ASI would need to meet this bar across virtually all tasks of human interest, not just some in narrow domains (which is already the case with some AI systems today that can beat any human in Chess and Go, predict the structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences, or prove theorems that resisted human mathematicians for decades). Interestingly, we have a good mathematical understanding of the very upper end of the intelligence continuum - the theoretical limits of general intelligence. We also know about hard physical, logical, and complexity-theoretic limits to what AI can achieve, such as predicting how real-world complex systems - from climate to immune systems to human societies - play out with arbitrary precision. Yet knowing those upper limits doesn’t tell us what comes before them. Even in theory, it’s hard to predict how capable a ‘good enough’ approximation of general intelligence can be. For example, solving chess perfectly requires far more computing power than exists on Earth, yet a thumbnail-sized chip can play the game well enough to defeat any human. What we do know is that fundamental limits lie far beyond both today’s AI systems and humans. But the vast space between human-level AI and theoretical limits to intelligence, which encompasses expert AGI and a whole regime of more and more advanced superintelligent systems, is largely uncharted. Cognitive industrialization Even if you are pessimistic that progress at the frontier of AI capabilities will continue, consider what happens if AI hardware and software continue to become more efficient. Over the last ten years, AI progress was fueled by steady growth in effective compute , driven by three compounding factors: Hardware manufacturing improvements: Under Moore's law and related trends, compute per dollar has increased by roughly 1.5x per year for six decades - meaning the same investment 18 months from now buys twice the compute. Algorithmic efficiency: The amount of training compute (FLOPs) required to reach a fixed AI performance level has fallen at roughly 3–6x per year over the last decade , while algorithmic efficiency at inference improved by roughly 3x per year. Doubling efficiency is practically equivalent to doubling the stock of physical compute. Compute hardware investment: Spending on AI hardware has grown by roughly 2.5x per year over the past decade. For example, the training compute of the largest frontier training runs grows by more than 4x per year . Multiplying all three factors gives an overall growth rate of global effective compute stock of at least 10x per year - a factor of 10 billion over ten years. Imagine that this trend holds. A decade from now, for each single AI agent you could run today, you would hypothetically be able to run more agents of the same quality than there are people in the world. At the same time, continued hardware and software (inference) efficiency improvements alone would reduce the compute demand to run an AI workload by about 4x per year . A cognitive workload that can be performed by today’s AI systems for $1 billion in compute tokens would cost just $1000 in ten years. Looking only at the last few years gives even steeper estimates: a recent Epoch study finds the consumer price for achieving a fixed score on a set of benchmarks has fallen by more than 13x per year since 2023. Extrapolating both trends into the next decade raises the prospect of a dramatically larger global effective compute stock combined with equally dramatic cost reductions for cognitive work performed by AI. Increasingly, many cognitive tasks may therefore soon become commoditised . Much like mechanical industrialization turned routine physical labor into a commodity, this shift will lead to cognitive industrialization characterized by rapidly increasing standardization and automation of cognitive work across sectors, industrial-scale infrastructure build-out, and an abundance of (certain) cognitive outputs and services. Is such a dramatic proliferation of intelligence realistic? It’s certainly not a given , but practical ceilings on compute build-out , and more speculative ceilings on algorithmic efficiency, together might allow the effective population of today’s AI agents to scale up by more than a thousand-fold by 2030, and more than a billion-fold within ten years from now. Would cognitive industrialization alone be enough to achieve ASI? If we froze other dimensions of AI progress and only scaled up today’s AIs in speed and number, the result might not even count as full AGI: there may still be cognitive tasks that AI cannot do without human help. Nonetheless, sheer scale can have a quality of its own . Suppose that we do achieve broadly human-level AI. Then there is clearly a major difference between human-level AIs that are slow and expensive to run, and a world where billions of agents act much faster than humans. That quantitative leap in speed and scale might itself be enough to bridge the qualitative gap from AGI to (weak) ASI. Unlike humans, digital intelligence directly benefits from more and faster compute in several fundamental ways: Processing speed: AI systems can reason, ingest data, and generate outputs at increasingly high rates. Working memory and memorization: Today’s models can literally memorize large parts of the internet and their working memory capacity far exceeds human limits. Substrate independence: The same AI system can migrate from one computer to another, upgrade to faster or more energy-efficient hardware, or run across heterogeneous, spatially distributed fleets. Lossless replication: Digital intelligence can be copied nearly instantly and without loss - not only its source code (akin to DNA), but also its memory state (our lifetime experience). Specialist systems can be trained once, then spawned in millions of copies when needed. High-bandwidth sharing of experiences: Humans must strongly compress experience and knowledge in order to teach others; AIs can replay stored high-bandwidth digital input-output streams across an entire population, and homogeneous AI groups could share raw learning signals directly. Four pathways from AGI to ASI Dramatically more efficient AI and larger compute stocks can scale up the speed and number of AI agents at a given capability level.

title: SmartPost AI: An AI-Assisted Framework for Intelligent Professional Content Creation and Automated LinkedIn Management
abstract: The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has had a significant impact on the area of AI-assisted content generation, providing capabilities to generate coherent context-aware text for different purposes. However, current solutions of AI writing assistants are limited in terms of addressing all aspects of professional content management, which include contextual information retrieval, organization, scheduling, persistent cloud storage, and automated publishing. Therefore, users are required to use several separate solutions, making their workflow less efficient and more labour-intensive. In this paper, we introduce SmartPost AI - an end-to-end framework for AI-assisted professional content creation and LinkedIn management. The framework utilizes the combination of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), LLMs, cloud-based data management, and LinkedIn API-based publishing, all integrated in one multi-layered architecture. The proposed framework enables users to provide either text prompts or web-based content, retrieve relevant contextual information, generate LinkedIn posts in professional format, convert Markdown output into Unicode-based formatting, and manage content centrally via secure storage, scheduling, and publishing capabilities. The framework is deployed as a cloud-based full-stack web application using Next.js, FastAPI, Supabase , and LinkedIn APIs. Deployment and experiment of the framework prove that the AI-based content generation, workflow orchestration, cloud storage, and auto-publishing features have been implemented successfully in one coherent framework. The suggested framework simplifies the process of content creation and makes it more automated, creating the basis for the intelligent AI-assisted content management and publishing system.

title: Reasoning on Call: Efficient Agentic Robot Control for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
abstract: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, allowing routine execution to remain with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions requiring additional assessment. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments further validate its effectiveness across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. Overall, RoC supports efficient agent intervention and coordinated recovery across execution and planning for long-horizon robot manipulation.

title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.

title: Validation-driven Deployment of LLM Inference Platforms for Agentic Workloads
abstract: Enterprises are moving agentic workloads from closed APIs to their own open-weight model deployments. For this reason, lifecycle-wide validation, from small-scale testing through sizing and pre-production to production, becomes all the more important. Typically, rollouts are evaluated with ad hoc tools whose accuracy is rarely checked. We present an end-to-end evaluation pipeline for agentic LLM serving and empirically ground the design choices that connect its stages. Our experiments show that replaying captured traces reproduces the per-session load of the original agent sessions: at the 95th percentile replay stays within 1.18x of the recorded input tokens while live re-runs reach 4.98x, so a small set of recorded sessions yields a repeatable per-session token load. A code-coverage analysis of vLLM further shows that the evaluated live, replayed, and synthetic workloads are complementary in this configuration: each exercises Python serving paths not reached in the measured runs of the others. In a case study rolling out four large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on llm-d, experiments show that the target models reached about half the optimal concurrency, and correspondingly about 60% of the throughput, on captured workloads compared with public traces. We open-source the relevant tools and release a trace dataset.

title: Static Analysis Guidance for Secure LLM Code Generation
abstract: Static analyzers are cheap and widely deployed, which makes their reports a candidate feedback signal for secure LLM code generation. Existing approaches place the analyzer inside an iterative repair loop with intermediate steps, which is costly and makes it hard to isolate the report's effect on the model. We introduce two strategies that give the finding to the model during generation. When the analyzer raises an alert, generation is rolled back, and the finding is inserted either as a code comment (Comment) or in the user message (Steering). We compare them with two iterative approaches and a control without the analyzer, across three models and three Python benchmarks, and we measure security using each benchmark's oracle. Guidance during generation is cheap and can be effective, at 0.9 to 1.9 times the baseline's output tokens against up to 24.1 times for iterative approaches. With DeepSeek-V4.1-flash on RiskyPy, Steering raises the share of functional and secure programs from 52.5% to 64.4%, close to the best iterative approach (66.2%) while using less than a fifth of the tokens. A per-rule analysis shows that rules with a local fix benefit most, and replacing the XML parser is net-positive on two of the three models. The study also identifies when guidance should not be applied. Analyzers flag at most 5.6% of the functional but insecure programs on SecEvalPlus, leaving little guidance to act on. When a static analysis alert (warning or error) contradicts the task, models tend to follow the analyzer and break the program. The two Qwen2.5 models often fail when the fix requires restructuring the code. These results indicate that static-analysis guidance is worth applying with a capable model, on rules with a local fix, and after filtering alerts that conflict with the task specification.

title: Self-Replicating Language Models
abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are a form of life is a scientifically interesting question. Under the Darwinian definition of life, it is also a practical one, because a system capable of Darwinian Evolution can adapt. We therefore test several modes in which a language model can reproduce itself: by emitting a genome that trains its offspring, by copying and mutating its own weights, and by teaching a child from its own samples. In principle, small language models can replicate and evolve: selection improves them, and they adapt to narrow niches. Selection also lowers mutation rates, and a language model, unlike any organism, can lower its own to zero, which may limit its evolution. Flagship LLMs can write such replicators, but for a large LLM to replicate by teaching its offspring remains, for now, technically and economically infeasible.

title: Streaming-AAA: Streaming AAA Game Video Generation at High Resolution, High Frame Rate, and Low Latency
abstract: Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.

title: Fold the Loop: Decoding-Time KV Memory for Looped Vision-Language Models
abstract: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen visual reasoning by repeatedly applying weight-tied modules. However, their decoding memory grows with recurrent depth and limits the image size and batch size that fit in a fixed memory budget. Each recurrent step produces its own key-value (KV) states, so the cache holds several copies of the same image. We find that, after an exact prefill, earlier steps still need access to visual information but can reuse the final visual KV within the same module. We propose FoldCache, which compresses visual KV along the recurrent axis while preserving the full prefill computation. FoldCache partitions recurrent steps within each module into groups and retains the final visual KV of each group for its members to share during decoding. Sharing stays within module boundaries, while question and answer KV remain separate for each step. The grouping granularity controls the degree of compression, and folding can be combined with token eviction and quantization to further reduce memory use. On LoopVL, FoldCache approximately halves prefix KV memory while matching full-cache accuracy on five open-ended benchmarks. These memory savings support batch sizes up to 1.7 times those of a full cache under the same GPU memory budget, and up to 2.6 times with the more aggressive FoldCache-Lite.

title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
abstract: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

title: Falsifiable Compositional Reasoning in Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Time series foundation models as well as the language-guided analytical agents achieve strong accuracy on standard chronological benchmarks. However, models that rank highest on historical validation splits often degrade across non-stationary regime transitions. We hypothesise that this gap arises from using historical backtesting as an open-ended search and model-selection objective instead of using it to test pre-specified compositional assumptions. Real-world time series are generated by recurring latent primitives that co-move within finite historical windows. Under strong historical co-movement, chronological holdout error cannot separate predictors that learn invariant couplings among primitives from predictors that fit transient historical correlations. Searching over large pools of architectures, hyperparameters, or chain-of-thought rules further biases selection toward historical shortcuts. Through theoretical analysis and diagnostic experiments on a controlled multi-primitive benchmark and German day-ahead electricity prices, we show that expanding validation search fails to improve out-of-regime accuracy, and that decomposing primitives without an ex-ante falsification test still breaks down when residual correlations shift. Hence, we propose formulating time series forecasting and reasoning around falsifiable compositional hypotheses that combine neural primitive encoders, explicit coupling constraints, and training-calibrated falsification tests.
